LADIES LETTER.
MY DEAR NELLIE,

For some time to come hats are expected to bs very flat—indeed, quite of the pancake type. Flowers have been worn all the winter, even on felt and cloth shapes, and the new models are quite garlanded with wreaths of gay spring blossoms, while white and light-coloured straw bats have already reale their appearance. Many winter hats are being smattened for spring wear by the addition of a draped scarf of white or ,-Team lace, entirely covering the brim and tied at tie back in a loose knot with short ends. The msjority of the new hats are much trlrnmed at the back, and display more or less elaborate arrange- ments of loops of velvet or clusters of flowers resting on the hair. A hat ef fine black straw trimmed with twists of black chiffon veiled with fine cream lace, and having a w!eath of blue forget-me-nots under the upturned brim at the back, ana a cluster on the low crown, is notice- ably pretty and far less inappropriate for the sea- son than are some of the Tuscan straw, coloured chip, and critic:line hats which all but fill th. windows of the modish milliners.

Fur is again cut up iato narrow bands this 'winter, and used in that way for trimming gowns, coats, and capes. A back satin dress has a deep• shaped flounce trimmed with five graduated bands of sable or mink. A removable bolero shows no fur at the back save the narrow turned-down collar, which is continued down the pointed fronts' but these fronts have each five hands of narrow gradu.• ated sable. A grey cloth gown is trimmed in very much the same way with chinchilla, hut with the difference that a narrow band of printed batiste in pale pink roses is stitched on above each row of chinchilla with tambour silver chiainstitch. A grey panne cape is worn with this, outlined with chinchilla headed with pink-rosed batiste in the same way. More within the Teach of everyday wearers is a grey cloth with rows of black velvet put on in graduated bands. This, like many of the new fas:hions, is a revival of one dating seine thirty years back.

Skirts coo '.n ~.?rease in fu7ness round the feet, but, while t;to top pani. admirably moulded round the hips, the lower prt from the knees downwards, st,ands out in a rounded way, like a bell, as if moulded out from the ;..a;:k, as one mole(' treat leather to get the rounded reliefs on the right side. Such an effect is probably done by a vast amount of damping, pressing, and pulling the cloth, and the skirt would require con- siderable support from underneath in the form of lining flounces. We can scarcely hope to keep the plain skirt with us much longer, for paniers and polonaise effects, accomplished by graduated flounces, have been threatening long. Neverthe- less, I am fully alive to the graceful potentialities of the full, flowing, plain skirt, and many may refuse to part with so becoming a garment at the dictates of fashion. There is no blinking the fact that big sleeves are returning to favour again, but at preseat the fulness is al/ below the elbow.

Coronation red and its near relation, a vivid cerise, are already marked out as colours which have a future before them.; but, for obvious rea- sons, they are not likely to find much favour amongst well-dressed people. Pale pink, of course, is always A favourite tint for batistes and zephyrs in the summer, .for nothing stands the sun better nor washes better, and it is generally becoming. But res4da green will be one of the leading colours of the spring, of a soft pasted shade verging on grey, which is highly attractive with a mixture of guipure ancienne.
Your loving JENNIE.

Brother B. J. Va.llender, Grand Master of the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows, WAS entertained to a complimentary banquet at qloucester the other evening, and presented with a gold watch and chain, a purse of £BO, and a gold and diamond brooch for Mrs. Vallender. The steamer Calabria arrived at Leith the other day from Riga, having experienced terrible weather in the Baltic. There were 45 horses stalled on deck, and many of them were washed out of their stalls and killed by heavy seas. Altogether 28 had to be thrown overboard.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The King when Prince of Wales, was frequently seen at the theatres, and His Majesty and Queen Consort, , accompanied by two or three members of the Royal ; Family, recertly paid their first visit t 3 one of tla, se ; Maces of entertainment, eitice the death of Queen j Victoria. The National Anthem was nit played, and many among the audience left the building unaware cf the presence of the Royal party. lint King's desire to follow this one of secrscy, as far as possible,when visit- ing the theatres, will be greatly welcomed by actors and actreEssts, who are apt to become distracted when half the audience or more are straining and casting side glances in • certain direction, to catch a glimpse of Royalty. When the preeence of the King and Queen are known, there is not only a demonstration, but this disturbance goes on througheut the performance, which ceases to be the principal subject of attention. Mr Balfour's proposal to alter the Parliamentary half- holiday from Wednesday to Friday, will have a distinct effect upon social arrangements in Sod ie ty circles, and the soggention is anything but welcomed at the fa bloc- able botela and restaurants. Wednesday has long been the one night of the week, during the London Season, for dinner partier,and social entertainments, and much of this gaiety is now threatened to be swept away. Friday can never take the same placeass the majority of our legislators would regard the half holiday as an in- ducement to spend the weekond out of town. The West- End shopkeepers are theretore up in arms against Mr Balfour's) proposal. In much the same way the Eden- burgh shopkeepers opposed the legislative union of England and Scotland, as that change did away with much social entertainitag in the Scottish capital. The season in Dublin promises to be a very brilliant one, and the first Drawing Room, which was held on Wednesday, was very largely attended. Nothing defi- nite his been anhounced about the King's visit to Ireland, and His Majesty does not encourage an intelli- gent antieipation of his arrangements amongst Court gossips and otters. The preparations at Dublin Caste all pint however to the probability of tne King and Queen Consort visiting Ireland before the Coronation, and it is believed that after that event, Lord Cadoesn will retire from the Lord Lieutenancy, which he has held for nearly seven years. This chaage will be greatly I regretted, as Lord and Lady Cadegan have teen very popular in Irish Society. Toe Musician" Company, it will be remembered, list year offered a prize of £5O, together with the freedom of the Company, for the best Coronation marabased the competition aroused considerable interest in musical circles. No fewer than 1.89 scores were sent in, and the 1 judges, Sir Frederick Bridge, Sir Hubert Parry, and Sir Walter Parrett, have selected one written by Mr Percy Godfrey, music master of ring's School, Canterbury. Par Godfrey, who thus becomes the prizewinner, is an ' Associate of the Royal College of Music, and a Bachelor of Music of Durham University. He is not, however, related in any way to the weli-known family of military bandmasters of the same name. He has already com- p Geed several pieces of music and no doubt his Coronation March will be published in due course. Lord and Lady Faversham have been advised hy the ' doctors ta send their grandson, the yout .ful Duke, of Leinster, en a long sea voyage The Duk , who is an exceptionally handsome boy ot fourteen, has been shoe - log signs of delicate health, and in view of the fact teat both his father and mother died of consumption, there is naturally some anxiety under these circumstances, about the lad'a constitution. His education has been superintended by his aunt, Lady Ulrica Duncombe, bet all studies are to be given up, and by the doetor's orders the Duke is shortly to co on a sea voyage, and devote himself entirely to open air recreations. The Duke I could not have been in betterthande for his upbringing, as Lady thrice, Huncombe not only trained as a hospital ' nurse, but she also gained much practical experience by her charitable work which she personally conducted amongst the very poor in the east of Loedon. Some of the most succe.sful miniature painters are ' womemand those who possess the genius of portraiture, are able to command very high Prices for their work. Miss Kiissner, an American lady, who divides her time between London and New York receives from £2OO to £4OO far her miniatures and amongst her sitters have been the Duchess of Marlborough, and Mrs Astor. Another very succsssful artist is Mrs Massey, who last year painted the childrea of the Prince and Princess of Wales. Mrs Massey has painted several miniatures of members of the Royal Family, and she is especially euccessful with children. Her miniatures of the little Princes and Princess were a present from the King to the Prince and Princess of Wales, after their return from their travels atrosel last year. There is, so rumour says, to be a re-actien this coming summer from the ethereal frock, worked up into im- portanee by atitchery, lace insertion, tucks, and elabora- tion on elaboration. Firmer toilettes are to be the order ot the day, an item which will delight the great maj ri y of women. and our home manufacturers. We all know bow costly the airy fairy gown can be, far more so for example, than one bulk of really beautil ul silk,ana what a differenee exists in the wear of these garments ! The dry diviners, and second rate modistes will of course deplore this change of ideas on the part of Dame Feshion, but the cbanee neverthele•s, will come. Very colt, rich, and lustrous are the English satins, MC4119, and moire salt que, so much in demand just now and the generality of women seem at last to have real. lied that English gilts are unquestionably better than the French varieties for dress foundations. The latter are cheaper it is true, but they cut,and wear cut in hqlf the time, and rustle aggressively. To much " rustle" and a combination of scents, are in the worst of taste. Regarding the latter, one powdered perfume should be ch.:cen, and used throughout the wardrobe. In flat sachets thia should be placed in various parts of the dress, when in course of erection, in under ' skirts and inside the lining of a toque or hat. This latter idea is an excellent one, as the powder acetate the hair delight- fully. Coloured shoes fcr evenicg wear are no longer donned , by wel -dressed women. Black and white are the beat worn, and these boast little in the we,' ot decoratien, a small rosette, a neat paste, silver, or cut steel buckle, or a diamond drop, being the meet approved. Tee bronze shoe is still worn,but this it seems will shortly disappear in favour of the gold specimen. Provided we continue ra, indulge in a touch of gold in our costumes, the gold Will give a pretty finish, but without this touah, the effect could easily be undesirable in the extreme. MADGE.

The Central News say—M? 51,rconi rrturns to America next month to complete his arrangements with the Canadian and United States Governments for an extensive installation of wireless telegraphy throughout the Continent. Within the next few months further operations in wireless telegraphy across the Atlantic will he engaged in on a, large scale, and as soon 58 com- munication is successfully established messages will be flailPd by wireless telegraphy from Great Britain to America at commercial rates.

At the great Protestant demonstrati,m in the Albert ndon on Tuesday night, presided over by Viscount Midleton, resolutions were enthusiastically adopted protesting against the steady growth of the Mass and confessional in the Church of England,mainly due to the Government's abuse of patronage,and stating that the inaction of successive Governments in allowing open violation of the law expressly providing for the exclusion of monks and Jesuits from residing in this country was unstatestnanlike, pernicious to society,and a danger to all good government. The speakers con- demned the introduction into thi3 realm of b,dies of erlebate militant Roman Catholic orders driven from their own country.

div.head: Husband Arrested on Suspicion.
div.p: Husband Arrested on Suspicion.

Alleged Lamp-Throwing. At the Warrington Police Court. on Monday, George Ball, a bricksetter's lahourer, living at 8, Appleton-street, was brought before Mr Monks (in the chair) and other magis- trates, charged with causing the death of his wife on Satur- day night by throwing a lighted paraffin lamp at her.—Mr eteel appeared for the prisoner. The Chief Constable said the facts were somewhat peculiar, and he should like to say at the out, et that there were as many facts which told in the prisoners fsvour as the undoubted fates which told against him. On aaturlay, , unfortunately, the prisoner and the deceased indulged; in a spree ..but in a quiet way. in their own house. They enter- tained at least two neighbours, one named Forster and the other a Mrs Griffiths, and beer seemed to have been sent for from time to time during the afternoon and evening, There was no history, absolutely no history, as far as the police had yet been able to ascertsin, of any quarrel or disagree- rnent,or of any bad blood beteen this man and the deceased. When they were left by Mrs Griffiths who was the last to see them before the unfortunate occurrence' they were sitting one on each side of the fire. Mrs Griffiths left shortly before half-past eight,and at 8.30 screams were beard issuing trona he house. Several neighbours rushed 113.90 Me by the , fro tt, and some by the back, and they found the woman in I flames. The pollee-officer who lived in the neighbourhood. P.C. Lewis, lauaied to the scene, and he found the woman in a state of great sulfating, and the man in a state of semi-collapse and half-dazed. The officer said " Mrs Bull, how did you meet with the accident le: The officer presume it Was art accident She replied ' "Ask my husband; he knows all about it." The prisoner made no observati on. Tim officer said : " Mrs Ball, how did you get burnt ?" and she answered: "My husband done it" The officer said a " How ?" and she replied : "He threw the lamp at me." At this time the man was near, , and when he heard what the woman had said he replied : " Yes : you can take me. lam willing to go anywhere. I never thought it would come to this." To that he (the ' Chief Constable) did not attach great imporeanoe, and as the man Was contused, excited, and admittedly In a semi- drunken state it might mean anything or nothing. Of course, the officer arrested the man, and telephoned for a horse ambulance, and it Was immediately in attendance. The offi er removed the woman with all speed to the Infirm- ary, but unfortunately, she died at 6 30 on Sunday morning. In the meantime an effort had been made to get her deposi- tio is taken before a magistrate. Mr Hayward and Mr White attended at the Infirmary, but the woman's condition was such that no depositions could be taken.—ln prisoner's presence at the Infirm ,ry deceased made a statement which Was practically a reiteration cf what she had said in the house. When the prisoner was taken into custody he denied throwing the lamp or being present when the accident happened. The case Was remanded until Friday morning. THE INQUEST. AN OPEN VERDIUT RETURNED.

I Tke inquest on the body of the deceased woman was , oonduoted at the Police Station on Tuesday afternoon by Mr I 8 Brighouse, County Coroner. A quantity of evidence was I called,af ter which the Coroner said the only evidence against the man was the statement the deceased herself made,but he Ifound nothing in the evidence to corroborate it. On the con- trary,it had been gradually impressed upon his mind that the woman was in such a state of drunkenness that she was not , very well able to exercise her mind and say veaat happened I (To the Chief Constable): Is there any information to corroborate the woman's statement? The Chief Constable : Absolutely none. The case rests upon the woman's statement entirely. Dr Mort, senior house surgeon at the Infirmary, deposed that the woman was fully conscious on admission into the institutton, but restless owing to the great pain she was suffer.ng. The deceased made a statement in the presence of her husband when the Clerk and hr Hayward, J.P., visited the Infirmary at eleven on Saturday night. As far as he recollected she said •• My master done it." By Mr Talbot : He did not attach any importance to her statement. He did not believe she kaew what she was saying. I At this stage the Coroner addressed the jury and said there [were a hundred and one things in prisoner's favour. He might have accidentally knocked the lamp off the shelf,or deceased might have done I) herself by suddenly rising from her feet They had no right to deprive prisoner of his i liberty by committing him for trial unless they were quite satisfied that there was a case to answer and that there was some substan,hl evidence.

The jury then left the court to conlider these points. On their return. in about three minutes, the foremen said the Jury did not wish to hear any more evidence. They had come to the conclusion th it deceased died from burns but how they were received there wee not sufficient evidence to show. The jury were diesatistied with the evidence of some of the witnesses. The Coroner : lam certain that one of the witnesses has not told us a'l she know.. A Juror : And one man was inhuman in not going t the deceased's assistance. The jury then returned a verdict of " Death from burns,' but added that there was no evidence to show under what circumstanees the injurtis were infinted.

The Chief Constable and the "Cabby."

At the Borough Pidice Court on Wednesday, before Mr T Birchall (in the chair) and Alderman Hutchinson. William Thomas Stevens, a cab driver was charged with having been drunk whil4t in charge of a horse and cab on Tuesday evening , He pleaded guilty.—The Chief Constable saki be 1 and his wife had been to the Court Theatre, and on leaving, looked for a cab to take them home. They fc.,un,l a hone and cab all right, hut no driver. After waiting ten minutes, the defendant was found by another driver, and they got into the vehicle They were driven 'up Bridge-street all right, and were ! then taken down Horsemarket•street and Scotland. road. The cab was going in a sort of zig-zag way, When they arrived home his wife was in a very nervous state,and be aslie.l the driver to Come down from the box, in order that lie might tee what con- dition he.was in. The defendant came down, but was so violent that the assistance of a gentleman named Duckworth was necessitated. Defendant used awful language, and was under the influence of drink. They had a great deal of trouble with him, but be was eventually got to the Police Station in a cab. When there it took four police- men to hod him—Defendant was fined 15s and costs.

div.head: TRAINING OF ALICE LOVEDAYI
div.p: THE TRAINING OF ALICE LOVEDAYI
BY MARGARET WATSON.
PART 1.-CHAPTER I.
It was an April afternoon. The sun shone warm in a pale blue sky, but round corners, and in the shade, a sharp little wind intimated that the nights of frost were not yet over. . . .

Two children were sitting in the sunshine, close to the trunk of a lime tree, whose shoots were redden- ing with returning life. A child of about two years old, with plump, red arms bare above the elbow—a curly, flaxen head, and blue eyes ; her little flannelette dress some- what soiled ; a tear in her pinafore. The other child was much older—a thin, dark girl with a gentle face. She was "in her fourteen" she would have told you, and tall for her age. The little one put her fingers in the tear in her pinafore: " 'Ook, Ally," she said, " Consty's pinny tore." "Never mind, dear. Alice'll mend it presently, when Mother's better—we mustn't go in now, else we should disturb her."
"When will Movver be better, Ally ?" asked the little one.

"Oh, very soon, I expect," answered Alice. At this moment a woman came out of a low, thatched cottage, at a little distance. The sun shone full in her face, and she shaded her eyes with her hand, looking up the road for the children. "Alice !" she said in a subdued voice, when she saw them, " come in and bring Consty—your poor mother wants to speak to you."

The tone filled -Alice's beart with a nameless fear. She got up from the ground, and, holding the little one's hand, came up to the woman and looked at her, with a wboite face and appealing eyes. "There, don't look at me like that, child," said the woman, her eyes filling with tears. "It do seem 'ard as you should be left with two babies as von mit say, and not much more nor a baby yourself— but there—'taint no use talking—you go along in and see your poor mother." Alice went in, leading the little one, through the brick-paved, low-celled cottage room, and then took the child in her arms to mount a crooked, worn stair-case, which went up from one corner of the TOM.

At the top of the stairs there were two rooms, Alice turned into the one on the right, and went up to the low, wooden bed on which her mother lay. Then she put the child on the floor, and, holding its hand, looked down, with fear turning her cold and sick, at the white face, with its great dark eyes, which looked appealingly up at her, and in Which she read something of fear too—. For the woman there was going out on a voyage over unknown waters, and leaving her little ones behind on waters whose perils she knew all too well. A little black lima and red face, lying on her arm, showed above the bedclothes.

"Alice," said the .woman in a weak, hollow voice. "Take care of the baby and Consty ; you've ails been a good girl to me—and thoughtful—you'll have to give up the school—but there,•that can't be helped. You'll do your best for 'em all—father and all—won't you. Alice 9" " Yes, mother—but oh it do seem hard as you 'shouldn't get wellwhy—" " It don't do to say ' why,' child," replied the mother, with a little more strength, " and p'raps baby might be took too—you could manage Consty and iather—" anti she looked at her baby, longing to take it with her.

" Oh, mother ! love the baby !" cried And then she broke down and sobbed aloud, end Consty cr:ed too, not knowing why, till they were hurried out of the room by the woman in charge. That night Mrs. Loveday died; and Alic, not quite fourteen years old, was left to take care of Consty and the baby-=a girl-baby—and "fe ther;" ' to wash, and cook, and mend, and lay out the tiny income to the best advantage ; for " father " had always depended on ," mother " for everything in- side the cottage door] He was not" handy" at ell, and tinderstood nothing of household finance., and it never occurred to him to wonder whether the young shoulders were too slight for the burden. He was a small, fair man, easy-tempered, and somewhat slow of intellect, but sticking to his own way obstinately on occasions.

The neighbours were very kind. Two of them took it in turns for a time to come in and dress the baby, for it did not die, but lived and throve. And. they would help with a day's washing now and again, when there were heavy things that Alice's small arms could not manage ; and they would ad- vise her about her marketing, taxing heavily their own small stock of spare time and strength to help the helpless little family. Among Alice's troubles, though she would not have spoken of it for the world—it was so inevitable —was the leaving school. She had lately been ap- pointed pupil-teacher, and she liked teaching the little ones, and had fully made up her mind that she would go on, and be " governess " some day, with a little house of her own, and a bit of garden, and. have Consty to live with her. Fortunately for her she had no time to spare more than a sigh for this titrangled ambition. The day's work was quite enough for the day. . The baby was christened "Ellen." Alice and the neighbour (Mrs. Giffkens) who had nursed Mrs. Loveday, were its godmothers; Loveday was the godfather. Alice made herself a perfect slave to he little Nelly. She was very fond of Consty, and very good to her, but Consty would be told sometimes to hold her tongue and be a good girl, or even (if persistent- ly troublesome when Alice was busy with the family wash) might get a box on the ear: but the baby had only to whimper and Alice flew to her—no mat:- ter if she was up to the elbows in the wash-tub, or in the midst of the absorbing intricacies of a boiled pudding for Sunday, the little trelly would be taken from her cradle at the slighteist indication that she was tired of it, patted, kissed, •and rocked in Alice's ams, and, if that were not enough, carried up and down the tiny room, the little head, with its downy dark hair nestling into Alice's neck, and the tiny fmgers getting entangled in her hair, while Alice sang over and over all the rhymes she could remem- ber till the dark eyes closed, and baby could be, with great care and caution, restored to the old wicker cradle. Mrs. Giffkens was a strict disciplinarian, and remonstrated sometimes at this over-indulgence "You may walk yourself to death with 'em if once you begins it, Alice—you didn't ought to get her used to it. If you takes her up every time as she cries, she's sure to cry every time as she wants to be took up." "I can't abear to hear her cry," returned Alice, "and she don't tire me."

" Well. I don't „know as I didn't feel like that over my first," admitted Mrs. Giffkens, "but you gets used to .'em when there's tree or four and don't fuss over 'em so. They gets heavier, "or you gets weaker, I expect," she added with a laugh. To Alice the moments when she held the baby in her arms were moments of pure joy, whether she walked up and down with it; or sat on a chair too high for her, with her feet tucked up on the front spar, touching the soft cheeks with her thin, bronn finger, and seeing her smiles reflected in the re- sponsive baby-face at night she would prolong the process of undressing to an unconscionable length, giving parenthetical attention to the untiying 9f strings for Consty and the unbuttoning of stiff little shoes.
And when both were in their white nightgowns she would lay the baby across her knees, and hold her little hands together, while Consty knelt and re- peated, lisping, after her :7-
"Now I lay me down to sleep, I pray the Lord my soul to keep, If I should die before I wake

10 take to Heaven for Jesus' sake.—Amen." And the to make all sure, an old prayer which their mother had learnt from her mother, and she from hers and so on, backwards to the time when .g,ngland was a Roman Catholic country :---
"Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, Bless the bed that I lie on,' Four angels round my he, Two at the Mot, two at the head:"
APT 11.

Two years passed, and Alice, at, sixteen. was ahrioit a woman. She Woe still thin, but not so thin, aad her Or of staid responsibility would have suited a AVOM:111 ipf twice her years. ' Her smooth, black ha'r no longer hung down !n elf-locks for baby fingers to clutch, bgt na. .neat: I twisted and coiled round her well shaped She had grown taller too, and no longer needed to put her feet upon the front spar of the 'chair when she had Nelly on her lap. She had assumed the full care of the family, and washed and ironed, and cooked and marketed like a grown-up Wonian. Consty, a far little slip of a girl, now went to school ; and the baby, the joy of Alice-'s heart, could toddle after her with uncertain steps and cry for " Ally " in intelligible tones. No one could help owning that Alice's pride in the baby was iustifia,blo- The first own of downy black

ir trad given place to son iifC7town curt; ti§) dark eyes were now dark blue, shaded by curling brown lashes; and the little red face had changed to that clear fairness which the sun loves to look upon, and will not mar with freckles, but touches to a warm brown. - And the child was as sweet-natured as she was pretty; even Mrs. Giffkens had to own that she.was not spoilt by Alice's over-indulgence. She 1111tuld sit on the cottage floor by the hour, playing with a few rough bricks, while Alice did her household tasks beside her, talking to her all the time, or sing- ing her favourite ballad about the fox who looked out one night and' "begged the moo 4 to give him light, For he'd many miles to trot that night Before he came to his den—oh."

And the child would babble scarcely articulate an. 13 were to the talk, or join in with the "den—oh "of die chorus. But into the peaceful, happy life came a disturbing element. Mrs. Giffkens took a lodger. He was a lad of eighteen, who had come from the next county to work for Loveday's master. His name was Ebenezer Clack, and he was called Eben for short. For the first day or two he did not hap- pen to see Alice. Then one afternoon as he was passing the lime-tree, which was slide favourits tine weather seat wills Alice when she had leisure to sit out of doors with ;N"elly, he saw her. She was dressed in a lilac-flowered print dress and white apron; her smooth coils of glossy black hair and the rich red and brown of her cheeks caught his atten- tion at once, and he noticed that her hands were busy with some knitting. The baby was at her feet gently whipping her knee with a twig from the bole of the lime tree, and as he came towards them, walking beside his team, ahe beat Alice more vigorously: " 'Ook " she cried. " Gee-gees !"

• Eben stopped his team: "Well, yoling 'ma," he said, approaching her. a But Alice's lip curled and her face flushed. Witt a toss of her head she rose, picking the child up 111 her strong arms, and marched off home, very angry that a strange young man should venture to address her baby as " young 'fin." She sat down in the cottage, and set the child on her knee, then she saw that her eyes were full of tears an her little lips quivering. "What was it then ?" she asked. "Did the naughty man frighten Nelly ?" " Nelly wanted to pat gee-gees," answered the child.

" Nelly shall pat Dadda's gee-gees—not pat naughty man's gee-gees." "Was he naughty man ?" asked Nelly, with wide open eyes. Eben ,watched Alice and the baby disappear into the cottage, then he said " Gee tout ' to his horses, and slowly moved on again. In the evening he questioned Mrs. Giffkens abowi her neighbours, and Mrs. Giffkens expressed the sentiments of the whole village when she told him: "There ain't a better gal than Alice Loveday let the next be who she may. The Way that gal ave took care of her father and they two children, and the one a baby not a week old—not but what us ha' done what we could to help her, and show her, and that—but there ain't many as would ha' taken to work like she ha' done—and as for that baby she wasn't nothin' but a white slave to it, and so I tolled her many's the time. But it ha' paid her—it is a nice child, and that I will say, and Alice thinks more on it I do believe then if she was its mother."

Next morning Mrs. Giffkens went across to Love. day's cottage.. Alice was busy washing. " Well, what do you think of your lodger ?" she -asked, clearing one arm of soapsuds with the finger and thumb of the other.
"He seems a quiet, civil-spoken chap—and clean and fresh-faced—but You see him yourself yester- day." •

Well, I didn't not to say me him. I didn't like the way as he spoke to baby, and him a 'stranger and all, so I jest picked her up and went in home." "Oh, he didn't mean no harm I don't expect. He was listing all about you last night. He snetaed to ha' in you. if you didn't see him." "He shouldn't be so free spoken," mid Alice, tossing her head. But on Sunday evening (Alice generally stayed at home in the morning to cook the dinner) when Alice, with the two children, called as usual at Lra. Giff- ken's, to walk down to. church with her, . she was surpr:sAl to find E ben leaning aghinst the door-post, as though waiting to accompany Mrs. Clitlkeris to vihurch. He was dressed ihi dark cloth clothe, and his face was fresher and cleaner than ever after his 'Sabbath ablutions. • " Good °Venni'," he said. " Goin' to church ?" " Yes. 1 always walks down with 31rs. CLif, kens." returned Alice with dignit);.. •
"We Mit Sig well-go She's jot cornin'," said Eben. " Shall I car' the child ?"
" Nelty don't like anyoue.but me to carry her," answered Alice.
But Eben was not tOle put down :- --
" You'll come to me, w'on't you, my dear F" he said holding out his arms to Neil. " I ha' got a little sister jest as bio as you be at 'on-Le."

The alluaon to a little sister, whom no doubt ho missed sadly, softened Alice, and Nelly actmlUy held out her little arms to him and let him take her wil- lingly. " Well I never !" exclaimed Alibe ; " I never maw her go to a stranger like that." But still she lingered, till to, her relief, Mrs. Giff- kens came out and exclaimed at the Laby's new lIIITBe.

So they all walked up the village streertogetlier, Mien carrying Nelly, Alice leading Censty, and Mrs giffkens with two little ones, one in esa hand. The word went round the village that Mrs -Giff kens' lodger was walking down to church carrying Alice Loveday'i3 Nelly. And the villagre said " Law !" •

But the -village grew accustomed to this sight; and accustomed too to see Ebenezer Clack start out after bis tea on a Saturday evening, and colic() back wheel- ing the perambulator which contained Nell y Love- day and the week's groceries, while Alice and Con- sty walked beside it. And the village was pleased to approve ; for it said he seemed a steady young fellow if ever there was one, and Alice did deserve a good husband if ever a girl did. Look at the part she'd done by those children and her father7--nOt but -what she Was young to be thinking of such things—but there— they didn't need to be in a hurry—they could wait.

div.head: LIVERPOOL BARMAIDS ADVENTURES. Remarkable Incident !n Kirkdale.
div.p: LIVERPOOL BARMAIDS ADVENTURES. Remarkable Incident !n Kirkdale.

The cage of a Liverpool barmaid, connected with one of the large commercial hotels, is f xciting a consider- able amount of interest, by reason of a peculiar experi- ence through which she has passed. Miss Elizabah Hilton, the young lady referred to, lives at 5, Luton- grove, Kirkdale, Liverpool, and particularly in this neighbourhood has her case created gossip. The occu- pation of barmaid is probably one of the most'exhausting occupations that a young woman could be engaged in. Not only are the hours long and late, but often during each day, when the houses an busy, the bartnai ds have 1 to be constantly on their feet, exercising both mind and body in fulfilment of their onerous duties. Then much of their time is spent in a heated atmosphere and amid the constant excitement aud noise of hotel life. A re- porter oalled on Miss Hilton t 3 glean particulars of her case,and found her a refined and ladylike young woman somewhat small of stature, with an intelligent face, and gentle manner and mode of speesh.

photograph by Vanderbilt, Liverpool.) Replying to the reporter's first question,: sue said she bad been in her present employment for srme years,and though she felt the work at times to be very trying, she liked it, and it was always full of change and variety. " I understand you have been ill, Mug Hilton. You might tell me something about it." " Well, you see, I have never, as long as I can re- member, had a very robust constitution. I never had much colour in ray cheeks, but I know I look better now than I did some time ago, as I was fortunately cured after a long illness by Dr Williams' pink pills for pale people, In March last I had a bad attack of influenza, and consequently became very weak ad low-spirited."

"That most have) been unfortunate. considering your occupation." " Yes- I was really very ii, and bad pains all over my body, with a splitting headeche at.d a feeling that I did not care what happened to me so long as I was allowed to reet. As you know, I leave a lot of running about during my working hours, and one is always ex- pected to be cheerful and nice ; but sometimes it took me all my time to attend to customers, and often I felt as if I must let business go unattended and have a good cry. I was at that time continually feeling tired and weary ; so much so that I often did not know what to do with myself. I suppose it is the way that influenzs affects people, but I sincerely hope it will never attack me again, I should not for tbe world like to go through tbe same experiencee a second time ; and I was begin- ning to feel so easily upset over little matters that formerly would not have troubled me at alle' "Did you not consult a doctor, or try something to make you better ?" " Oh, yet, I am coming to that. I tried many so- oal:el remedies for the depressing effects of influenza, but did not derive the least beneft from them. Do what I might I could not shake off the effects of the influenza and regain my etrengtb,snd I continued to be just able to drag about. At last I began to get rea Ic alarmed about my state, feariog that I might have to leave my employment entirele. But just at this time, when my spirits were at their lowest ebb, I was talking with a friend about my illness, and how hopeless I ' seemed to be of getting anything which would make me better. During the conversation my friend asked me if I had ever tried Dr. William' pink pus for pale people, and I laid no—that I was sick. and tired ot trying remedies, which had cone me no good. Well, my friend was so urgent and anxious that should try D. Williame pink pills, and gave me several instances of remarkable cures effected by them, in cases similar to mine, that I promised to give them a trial. Next day I purchased a box of the pills, and took them faithfully according to the instructime, and I can honestly say that by the time the box was finished I felt that I was decidedly better. At last, I thought, I urn on the right way to recovery, and I got twe more bex-s of Dr. Williams' pink pills. I then began to ineptieve rapidly, and when the third box was finished, I feet nearly as well as ever " " Did von stop taking Dr. Williams' pink pills then ? ' " No. I was determined to guard against any recur- rence cif the trouble, so I persisted with the pills for some time longer. As I continued to fate them the low and depressed feeling vanished, I began to take more interest in affairs, and my appetite—which had become very poor—improved. I Continued to gain strength." now many boxesilsave you taken altogether 2" '• Lave taken six boxes in all, and am now well and strong in fact, I feel better k in:l7s for rapn lenypeernlphleabv7e. clone as long as I can rememb.s. lam always going to keep a or of Dr me, and will take them should I feel not very well at any time. I bless the day my friend made me promise to try Dr Wiliam' pink pills, end though I will confess I did sot think they would do me mucti good when so many other se-called rem,die had failed, I can now truly say they acted like rnagic,and made me have new hopes and interests in life." " Do you know of any others who have derived bene- fit from Dr Williams' pink pills for pals people 2" " Oh, yes, since my own cure I have never lost an opportunity of telling people about the virtues of the pills, and in every case where they have tesn taken the patients have derived greet benefit. In fact, like myself, they all say that Dr Williams' pink pills tre among thcir most valued possessions."

The amount raised during the four days was £3lO and we are told by the Manager (Mr A Downes), that this is a second sum for any single town Tne Manager wishes to express his thanks to all who Nndered assistance in any way. A Fatal FM*-I.

. An inquest was held in the Coroner's Court at the new Police Station, on Tuesday afternoon, on the body of John Ho!croft (S 3 a trope spinner, who lived at 1, Pinner's-brow. On the night of the 4th December the deceased was in his bedroom retiring to rest when he fell on the fender, fracturing his skull. He died on alonday last. A verdict of accidental death was returned.

The Coastguard Station on the Scarborough Caste Hill has been turned by the War Office into a war signalling station. The signaller commenced duty on Mrmday, and watchers will be kept daily on duty from daylight to dusk. When the fleet. mobilises, and in times of emergency, the station will be open day and night. DID THE CAT .1 KILL BABY —Roberts' Kitchener Bunker, aged eight mcntiv, whose fatter is serving in S9tHll Africa, has died in a very mysterious way at Poplar. His mother laid him down on the bed to sleep, but when she went to pick him up he was dead. There was a cat in the room, and at the inquest on Tuesday Dr William Skelly slid death was due to suffocation, and the only cause he could suggest was That the cat had interfered with the child in some way. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidentaldeath."

div.head: Caarrin 111.
div.p: Caarrin 111.

But the time came when Ebenezer Clack —at twenty—(Alice was eighteen) got the offer of a tet- -4r ter situation and. a rise of wages, at a lace 'ever so far off—right at the other side of don. A brother-in-law had secured it for him, an wrote that he ought not to miss it... . ..

' Th; letter came in the long da•27B of June, when all the world (Eben's world aiSid Alice's) was hay- making. The whirring mowing-machine cut the flowerlia,g grasses, with the ox-eyed daisies and the red sorrel, into long swathes' and then the tedder came anti tossed and spread it over the field, and after that the horse-rake, with its enormous teeth, raked it up into rows again, and then it was the women's turn, who made the rows into large, sweet smelling cocks. div.head: EVENTS OV. THE WEEK
div.p: EVENTS OV. THE WEEK
ILLUSTRATED,

After two-and-a-half anxious years of hostility, rumours of peace are a pleasant change from rumours of war, and the whole nation was agog after Mr. Balfour's statement in the House last week that certain suggestions were before the Cabinet. Since then, although the Government have not seen their way to fall in with them, and have felt themselves reluctantly obliged to refuse the proffered mediation, the main outline of the story has come out, and it shows us that Holland, which has, taken .all round, shown itself wonder- fully impartial during the whole War, despite its close kinship to the Boers, is eager to help in establishing peace, but—and here came the crux—they have no credentials, no authorised commission from the other side. As Lord Rosebery truly said, ,Dr. Kuyper, the Dutch Premier, did not run over to London recently to inspect the "old masters," much as he may admire art, but for the practical political purpose of sounding certain people unofficially, and owhether it be the Liberal ex-Premier, Lord Reay, or sotnebody else at the bottom of it, the immediate result of his informal trip was

div.head: DR. ICHYPER, THE DUTCH PREMIER
div.p: DR. ICHYPER, THE DUTCH PREMIER

WHO IS ENDEAVOURING TO RESTORE PEACE IN SOUTH AFRICA. the Dutch offer of mediation. It was certainly a dignified and friendly effort to bring about the end of hostilities, and, had it not been for the lack of authorisation, it might have led to some real result, as everybody—Boers, Dutch and Britons alike— know the essential points the Cabinet have laid down. If the Boers were avowedly willing to com- ply with these, who can doubt that the Government would be only too glad to welcome peace? Any- how, the effort of Dr. Kuyper and the Dutch Government, failure though it may have been in actual result, is a step in the right direction, and may ultimately bear fruit to the advantage of both Briton and Boez.

It has long been patent to the most superficial politician that the Parliamentary machine was decidedly rusty and out-of-date, and it caned little surprise and no displeasure when Mr. Balfour, as Lea-der of the House. announced last autumn that one of the Government's first tasks in the next cession would be the overhauling and adapting of it to modern requirements. In the old days the floor of the House was for the most part held by a few select orator S and active legislators of established standing„ but during the last half century, and especially during the last decade, the ordinary M.P. has realised that there was no reason why his voice should not be heard in our natiotal legislative assembly, or the needs of his pArticular constituents not be brought before the notice of the nation. Hence the speaking Member has become the rule rather than the exception, until neither time nor space has proved able to contain him, and this overhauling has become a necessity of modern development to ensure the irreducible minimum of public business being transacted. Mr. Balfour, therefore, as Leader of the House, has taken the bull by the horns and has laid down an outline of procedure, which will relegate everything to an appointed niche, assuring as far as possible a time and place for everything, and everything being in its time and place. Under the new rules the House will meet at 2 p.m. Mondays, Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays, and sit till midnight, adjourning from 8 p.m. to 9 p.m. for dinner, whilst on Friday it will meet at noon and sit till 6 p.m., adjourning at that hour till the following Monday, thereby admitting of a little relaxation, golf or whatnot, for the jaded Government and private Members. Private business is to be taken from 2 till 2.25, after which it must stand over till the evening. Next, five short minutes are to be allowed for
THE NEW RULES OF PAULIAMF.NTARY PEOCEpERE
'SITE RT. EON. DALroun EXPLAINING TOE GOVERNMENT'S
PRVPOSAL.

urgent questions relating to the business of the House, and at 2.30 punctually the debate on the question before the House will commence. At 7.15 questions will be resumed until the adjournment for dinner, a step which will release non-curious private Members at that hour. At nine, any re- mains of private business will be disposed of and then public business will be resumed. Only one supplementary question is to be allowed to every one on the paper, instead of an ad libitum number, while unnecessary divisions are to be avoided. Disorderly conduct is to be dealt with in a more drastic manner than formerly, twenty days' suspension being the penalty for a first offence, forty for a second, and eighty for a third, and any part of such a sentence not com- pleted at the end of one session is to be worked -off at the beginning of the next, to prevent any shirking. Mr. Balfour's scheme is as follows : Afternoon Sitting. Evening Sitting. Government. Government Private Members.

Under this new re'aiiiie the work of the ,House will be more systematic, and Members will have the advantage of knowing exactly what is coming on next.

div.head: AN INTERESTING ENGAGEMENT.
div.p: AN INTERESTING ENGAGEMENT.

and it was during Lord Roberts' command in the Emerald Isle, which he gave up to proceed to the front in December, 1899, that Lady Aileen Roberts and her future husband first met. In South Africa they met again with the happy eventuality of the present engagement, upon which everybody will congratulate them most heartily, and offer them thery good wish, not only for the father's, but for their own sake. Any issue that may result from this marriage will continue the earldom which the Commander- has so honourably won by his great railitary career, which ha crowned by his splendid success in South Africa.

To the complete surprise of many people, especially in North Britain, the team captained by E. Gwyn Nicholls of Newport, vanquished the representatives of Nicholls, in fine style in the great Rugby match at Cardiff on Saturday. Scotland, playing practically the same team that did such brilliant work last season, felt very confident about disposing of the Welshmen without a great deal of difficulty, but the gallant little Principality is a hard nut to crack when its defenders have native soil beneath their feet, as Scotsmen have previously found. In fact, it is ten years since Scotland won an International on Welsh ground. The most significant feature of the game was the complete mastery which the Welsh forwards gained over their old rivals, whose reputation for superiority in this department is a hoary-headed tradition, On Saturday the Scottish forwards collapsed before the magnificent work accomplished by their opponents, and with a splendid back E. G. NICHOLLS, THE WELSH CAPTAIN.
J. I. GILLESPIE WHO SCORED THE ONLY GOAL POR SCOTLAND
THE WALES v. SCOTLAND RUGBY MATCH AT CARDIFF.

division the first twenty minutes saw th Welshmen run in four tries and place a goal, while Scotland had only succeeded in register- ing one goal, which was kicked by Gillespie. The second half, although productive of some capital football, saw no change in the score. Now that Wales have beaten ngland and Scotland, their prospects of gaining the triple crown are extremely rosy, but we have yet to see what Ireland will do. To glance at the Association game for a second, the Most remarkable,event in the First League series of matches took place at Birmingham, where Sunder- land beat Aston Villa by a goal to nil. The great event of the theatrical season is the production on Saturday night at Her Majesty!s Theatre, by Mr. Beerbohm Tree, of Mr. Stephen Phillips's blank verse play Ulysses, which is the greatest effort in literary drama that has been given to the public for many long years. The dramatist, who has established for himself the position of one of our leading living ,poets, has already scored a success on the stage in Herod, also produced by Mr. Tree, and for this reason his second hostage' to fortune was eagerly looked forward to. Now that it has come, it is hard to say whether it was a disappointment or not. To such a select audience of " first-nighters " it undoubtedly appealed, but whether it will do so to the public at large is another question. The piece consists of a prologue —a rather unnecessary discussion amongst the gods on Olympus as to the fate of this Ulysses who has angered Neptune by blinding his son, Cyclops and three acts. The first shows Telemachus, Ulysses' young son, entertaining perforce the suitors for his mother's hand on the Island of Ithaca; the second depicts the wanderings of the god-driven hero, especially in his temptation by Calypso in her cave and his descent into Hades; and the last concludes the play with his return home in disguise, after having seen many men and cities, at the critical moment. The old Homeric tale is faithfully adhered to in all the main points, and naturally recalls the Odysseus, while Mr. Stephen Phillip's blank verse is very strong and. resonant. But it is a play of elocution rather than acting, and there is not great scope for Mr. Tree and his company, but it is superfluous to say that they do all possible with their parts.
MISS NANCY PRICE.'
MR. BEERBOHM TREE.
THE PRODUCTION OF " ULYSSES " AT HER MAJESTY'S.

The fault from a dramatic and spectacular point i of view s alack of action in the main. Mr. Beerbohm Tree, :vlio is worst always in sentimental and emotional rolev. is not very well suited by the part of Ulysses. but acts with enthusiasm and sincerity. Miss Lily Hanbury, makes a delightful Penelope, and Miss Nancy Price, who plays Calypso—vice Mrs. Brown Potter, resigned—is an admirable and most seductive goddess, difficult to resist. Miss Constance Collier is rather too robust for one's conceptio4 of Minerva, but shines as an elocutionist, while Mr. i Fulton is a majestic and i thundering Zeus. But t son the whole a thank- less task for the actors engaged, and praiseworthy as is a revival of drama in hexameter and an, attempt at the lost art of verse diction, it should; not be at the expense of opportunities of acting., Needless to say the mounting is superb, it a littJW reminiscent of Drury Lane at Christmas in pieces,.

div.p: Bold-street Wesley Guild.

A devotional meeting, in which varius members of the guild took part. V7RB he/d in the Wesleyan School on Monday, the Rev WC JI Neville in the chair. The subject for discussion was " Busines. and the soclal ronnd in its relation to the higher life," This was very ably dealt with by Mr L'ttler.
GYMNASIIC DISPLAY AT WARRINGTON.

There was a good attendance of the public at the Parr Hall on Monday evening, when the fifth annual gymnastic display and miscellaneous enter tainment in connection with the Warrington 'Gymnasium was held. An exceedingly interesting programme had'been arranged and the proceedings passed off without a hitch. The members of the boys' 'lass opened the display with a dumb-bel exercise which was given with complete accuracy Another vouthful contingent thee pleased the audience with an exhibition of their skill on the horizontal bar, and this was followed by a clever vaulting performance by members of the senior class. Four pupil; of Miss Ethel Spin ks then con- tributed a charming Old English Dance, and this was one of the most acceptable items of the even- ing. The girls were attired in pictur- esque costumes and acquitted themselves so admirably that a vigorous demand for a repeti- tion had to be complied with. The promoters of the concert bad done well to engage Mr Nelson Jackson as the humorist of the evening. He is quite a favourite with Warrington audiences and on Monday evening he kept his hearers in roars of laughter with songs and anecdotes given in his own inimitable way. Other items on the first part of the programme were a bar-bell exercise by the girls' class which vvas very creditably submitted and the song " be carries the gun?" by a number of boys from People's College. Too much praise cannot be bestowed upon the boys who appeared in the last named selection. They were clad in khaki costumes and the striking feature of their performance was the military drill which was executed with marked precision. Sergt- Major Rawlinson, of the Volunteers, was responsi- ble for the training of the boys for the drill and their exhibition reflected credit upon their tutor. The second portion of the entertainment was of equal interest to the first. The members of the senior class gave an exhibition with the Indian clubs, and other pupils of Miss Spinks executed a very pretty Algerian dance. An original feature was the blind fold boxing by Messrs Holloway and Parr. Mr Nelson Jackson scored a pronounced suc- cess in a humorous musical sketch and the enter- tainment wound up with a number of feats on the parallel bars by the boys', girls', and men's classes. Miss A Clayton ably discharged the duties of pianist and Mr Kinaley as usual,directed the exercises.

At the last meeting of the Institution of Civi Engineers, Mr William Spinks, lecturer on sanitary engineering at the Yorkshire College, was trans- ferred to the class of members. Mr Spinks is the eldest son of the late Dr Spinks, and served his articles in Warrington with the late iiar R Vawser, M,I,C.E. The framways C3mmittee of the Salford Corpora- tion have passed a resolution re-appointing Mr E Batton as general manager and engineer of the tramways for a further period of twelve months, at a salary of £450 per annum. Mr Hatton was formerly in the en ploy of Messrs Pearson and Knowles, Warrington. 1 Mission in the Parr Hall. A great effort was put forward on Sunday night on the occasion of Mr Joe Corbett' s Evangelical Mission, and the town was aroused by the appro- priate music with which the Legh-street Brass Band provided the general public. There was a good gathering at the ball, which was encouraging to the promoters of the mission and especially to the evangelist himself, on whom the greater part of the organizition of the services had fallen. The services of the Warrington Male Voice Choir were very much appreciated, and they are to be compli- mented on their excellent performance. There was also a large choir in attendance. At the opening of his sermon Mr Corbett pointed out that he had not come to preach the Wesleyans, Baptists, Primitive Methodists, nor any other distinct sect, but he had come with a desire to proclaim the true gospel to rich and poor, high and low ; no matter whether they went to church or not. He did not want to preach to the regular church goers ; it was to those who did not go to church at all to whom he princi- pally wanted to speak,and it was his earnest prayer that the resuLt of his effort would be that he would at least have the satisfaction of knowing that, in response to his entreaties, be would be the instru- ment in God's hands, and through God's help, in converting many people outside the church to a higher and nobler iife.—lt is to be hoped that the successful service held on Sunday night will only be the forerunner of many more and even greater successes, and that it will be the means of creating new energy amongst Christian workers, and better- vg the spiritual life of- our town.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
COUNTY MATCH.

DURHAM AND NORTHUMBERLAND v. LANCASHIRE. Playeu at South Shields on Wednesday afternoon, before 3,000 spectators. Lancashire started, and in some splendid passing nearly scored. Durham neat rushed play. Hector kicked a penalty goal. Lancashire then scored through Fish, W James converting easily. Lancashire vigorously attacked Durham being outdone in passing. Fish ran in a try, W James anin kicking a goal. The latter added a penalty goal. Hector followed suit for Durham. Then W James landed another penalty goal. Half-time :—Lancashire 14 points. Durham and Northumberland 4 points. The second half was well contested for the first ten minutes. Then the Durham combination went all to pieces, and the visitors scored as they liked. Tries were put on by Hampson, Fish, W James, Whitehead (2). Heath and Bowker, Swainson and Archer scored for the home county. W James scored four goals and Fish three. Result •---Lancashire 49 points, Durham and Northumberland 10 points.

div.head: NORTHERN LEAGUE.
div.p: NORTHERN LEAGUE.

HALIFAX V. LEIGH. At Halifax, before 5,00) spectators. The ground had been protected, and Was in good condition. At the interval Leigh led by a goal to nil. Halifax had the wind in the second balf, and they pressed hard. Nichol' eventually scoring an unimproved try. Little afterwards placed a penalty goal. Davies next ran three-quarter the length of the field but was overtaken by Rigs just (outside the line after the best) sprint of the day. Soon after the start of this game at Hull the home team scored by the aid of good passing. Jacques placing the goal. Bradford made strenuous efforts towards the close, but no further scoring Book place. the result being :—Hull, one goal and one try (five points); Bradford, one goal and one try (five points).

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
A W ARRINGTON BIGAMY CLSE-PRTRONER COMMITTED FOR TRILL.

At the Warrington Police Court. on Tuesday. before Mr Robert Garnett (in the chair) and Alderman Hutchinson, William Bromley, of Newport. Monmouthshire. was char.-1 with having committed bigamy by marrying Ruth McLean Blenkinsop, who resides at 16, Smith-street, Warringten whilst his former wife was yet alive.—The Chief Constable said It was not of ten that they had within the four corners of a charge of bigamy facts which were so direct, and which were so short, tie might say that the prisoner fully admitted his guilt, and realised the seriousness ot his position. ellss Ruth McLean Blenkinsop was in 1900 a young woman, 25 years of age. and lived with her mother, whom she helped to maintain, at 16, omith-street. She was a fustian cutter. , One night she was in Bridge-street and the prisoner, who belonged to that class of persons who did not require the formality of a sooiety introduction to make themselves known to each other, struck up an acquaintance, and the result was that the wan asked to be ahowed to keep com- pany " with her. Permission was gives, and the two walked out together. Subsequently, matters assumed a more business-like appearance. and Bromley visited Mrs Blenkin- sOp's house as her daughter' accepted suitor. Things went on until they were married at the Parish Church,Warrington on the 29th December, 1900. The marriage was celebrated by the Rev A F White in the presence of of Sarah Ellen Stringer, who acted as bridesmaid, and Mr Lloyd, the parish clerk. They went to live at 32.Wellington- street, as man mud wife, end continued to do so until the 26th of April. 1931. when prisoner went out of the house and failed to return. The wife was alarntPd and distressed at the absconding of her husband, and made futile enquiries as to what had caused him to go. She received a letter, it was not material who or where from, which caused her to make further inquiries, and as a result she found that be was a married man, and had a wits and three children living in Monmouthshire.—Bvidence having been given Bromley was committed for trial at the next Liverpool Assizes.

ALLEGED THEFT BY 311V-;;;VO'F—A TRICIC.—WiIIiaM Mackie 2, Ship-yard, was charged with tstealing by means of a trick the sum of 30s, the moneys of William John Laird. on Satur- day evening; and also with stealing a horse's bit,of the value of 3s, the property of Joists Maginn.—The Chief Constable said prisoner came from Manchester. He had no regular employment, but did odd jobs for various people, including Mr William John Laird. On Saturday night at about seven o'clock, Mr Laird was about to go' into Messrs Cooper's stores to pay a bill when be heard an express train corning into the station. As he wished to catch that train he gave the prisoner a bill, and a sovereign and a half sovereign to go and pay the account, which amounted to Zels, telling him to bring the change to the cab stand or to the station. That was the last he saw of him. Mr Laird subsectriently went to Mr Cooper and found that the bill had not been paid and prisoner had never been there. A cab- driver named Littlewood, hearing that prisoner had bridled with the money went on the platform about 7.50 when the trains for Manchester and Liverpool were due out, as a sort of amateur Sherlock Holmes. He saw the prisoner and asked him if he had paid atir Laird's bill, He replied. " Cer- tainly, I have paid it " Littlewood had his suspicions and communicated them to P.C. Monks, The constable went on the station and not being satisfied. Vie man was taken to the Police Station. where it was found that he had net paid the bill. On being searched, 27s in money was found on prisoner, he having spent the re- mainder in drink and in buying a ticket to take him to Manchester. He had attempted to destroy the ticaet, but it had been recovered. With regard to the second charge, the horse's bit which had been identified by Mr Magina as belonging to him, was found in possession of the prisoner, who said he had bought it in Manchester.—The man was remanded until to-day (Saturday ) CRUELTY To I HORSE.—Th4mas Sutton, 18 Fennell-street, was oharged with having ill-treated a horse by causing it to be worked whilst in an unfit state, on the 18th January.— Mr. Steel prosecuted on behalf of the R.S.P.O A., and said the horse was lame on both hind legs, but more so on the near one. There vras considerable heat inslie each hock. The animal was in great pain and quite linable to work.— Inspector Print corroborated, and defendant who said he had only had the horse a short time, was fined ss.

A LANCASHIRE CASE THAT IS TALKED ABOUT. Weakness and Indigestion Threatened Consumption. The Trouble Banished.

The congenial climate of Sunny Southport appeals largely to the workers of the County Palatinate and thousands are invigorated by visiting this favourite watering-place. A somewhat extraordinary instance has just come to light where even the ozone-laden breezes of Southport failed to do just what was required. Mr er ames Quinn, of 11, Hollins-street, Stalybridge, foundryman, has had this experience He r dily and intelligently related it to an" Oldham Standard "reporter, who waited upon him. . Mr. Quinn, who is forty-seven years of age, is a native of Stalybridge, and until of

recently, had spent the greater part of his working days in the mill and the foundry. "For the past twenty years," he said, "I have been plagued with indigestion. The principal cause of it was that I fan myself down when working in the foundry. I used to sweat in front of the furnace, go home to dinner and hurry back again, the varying tempera- ture leaving its mark in the long run. I began to suffer from general debility and excessive weakness, and got so much worse that I determined to see a doctor, who told me that if I did not at once go to Southport consumption would probably develop. " I went to Southport, staying three weeks in the Convalescent Home there, but nothing did me so much good as Dr. Williams' Pink Pills. I certainly felt a little better while at Southport, but it did not revive me like the pills." Mr. Quinn went on to state that he felt as well to-day as ever he had done, and, as he certainly appeared to be in good health and spirits, the reporter was tempted to probe into the nature of Mr. Quinn's suffering. • " Every time I ate anything,' he explained, "I had wind on the stomach, and I had such a painful weight in that part that at first I used to force my food back again. My strength gradually failed me and I became very tired and depressed. '''Then I became so much run down that the doctor feared I would go into consumption." "How did you first come to hear of Dr Williams' Pink Pills ? the interviewer asked. "I happened to be complaining about my indigestion to a young fellow at Ashton' when he asked me Do you think Dr Williams' Pink Pills will do you any good ?' I started laughing at him and then answered, They are the same as everything else ; they give temporary relief, and then you get as bad as ever.' He told me he thought they were as good a remedy as I could get, and, thinking about what he had said, I ultimately determined to give then/ a trial. When I had been taking them a week I felt great relief. I kept on with them, and they took the pain away. Of course, I had to regulate my food at the same time, but I found that Dr. Williams' Pink Pills did me a deal of good. I continued taking them until I had finished two boxes, when I felt in very fair form, and stopped taking them. I have not needed to have any for the last three months, being now free from indigestion, and deriving good benefit from my food."

div.head: ASTONISHING CASE AT PRESTON. ,

A Physical Wreck from Nervousness and Sleeplessness.

singular experience was that of a Preston woman, Mrs Helme, of No. 6, Emmett-street g Ao did not sleep either night or day for three months. Mrs Helme's case created a lot of interest among all who heard of it. Speaking to a reporter about it, she stated: "Yes, it is quite true," said Mrs Helme "I was so bad that I used to come downstairs in the middle of the night and wander about the house in a distracted state. Of conrse I got weaker and weaker, and was at times perfectly tielpless. At last I took to my bed for good, as I thought, as I never expected to get up again. I had two doctors, one after the other, and the second one said I must get up and drag myself, however painful it might be, into the street, if I wanted to live. My vitality had been reduced so low, and I was in such an extremely depressed condition that I did not care to live, I had been suffering on and off for six years with a bad stomach, indigestion,weak action of the heart, and weakness generally, and I grew worse and worse, till my nervous system seemed to be completely wrecked." "How did you come to regain your apparently healthy condition ?" " We never thought she would live," now put in her husband," but one day a friend came in and said, Why don't you give them a trial ? ' referring to an article in the papers about Dr. Williams Pink Pills:' "We took the advice and sent for a!box." said Mrs. Helme,resuming the narrative. "I soon began to feel much brighter, and I cared for my food. For five years I had not been able to do anything, but I persevered with the pills, and now, as you see,l am well and strong again. I take them on and off yet when I feel a little out of sorts. The indigestion has left me, and the action of my heart has grown much stronger, while the distressing nervous- ness, which prevented me from sleeping, has entirely gone, and I can now sleep and rest well. Altogether I feel a different person."

div.head: TOO ZEALOUS HOUSEMAID
div.p: A TOO ZEALOUS HOUSEMAID

Energy is a delightful thing, quite natural to the young, though it sometimes needs more intelligent direc- tion thee its owners can give it—as in the case of the too zealous housemaid who, in cleaning her master's study, destroyed all his manuscripts acd correspondence in the belief that paper when once it was writteß upon was of no further use. (The remarks made by the gentleman on discovering this clearance have not been recorded). But energy, whether wisely or unwisely directed, denotes health ; and when young people are without it, something is wrong, and calls for remedy. Miss M Stonier,of 16,Essex-street,Bootle,Liverpool is a young lady whose youthfulness should be a sure warrant ' of energy and joyousness. But foe°, long time these bless- ings were denied to Wes Stonier, who thus wrote on July 10th, 1901 : " Some time back the state of my health occasioned me much concern. I was oppressed by a tired, drowsy feeling, and all energy seemed to leave me. My cheeks became pale, and I grew weaker and more listless daily. !lad I been able to eat, I think It would have been better for me; but, unfortunately, I had no relish far anything, and the little I took occasioned me severe pain in the chest. My drowsinees was so extreme that the desire to lie down to rest was continually upon me ; and yet, when I did so I was often unable to sleep, and arose feeling even more life- less than when I went to bed. Being quite at a loss what to do, I began to fear that I should never get well again. It so happened that just then my father was taking Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup for indigestion, and as he derived great benefit from it, he persuaded me to give it a trial. lam very thankful that he did se. Its effect upon me was such that I felt brighter and better from the very first, and by the time I had taken four bottles of it,l had regained my health and strength. I can safely say there is to better medicine in the world than Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup for the cure I of ansernis and indigestion." Miss Stonier's case is typical of a very large class of similar cases. With the continual growth of town life, and desertion of villages and farms, it seems not impro- bable that annemia will become more common than ever It is a malady to be vigilantly guarded against, not so much for itself (though the person afflicted with it can have little or no pleasure in life) as for the condition of enfeeblement which it sets up. Careful watching of the general health, fresh air, generous did, exercise, and the medicine recommended to Miss Stonier by her father, may be relied upon to preserve the energy of youth.

Howard, for several montus engaged in the same cam- paign, was wounded at the battle of Burghersdorp. and returned home invalided. He has since resumed police duty, quite strong and well. P.C.Muskett is again on service with the Garrison Artillery.
