The Dutch correspondence The Dutch Offer, with eur Foreign Office, which was published this week, has ended without any apparent result, though it may yet prove exceedingly fruitful. In the first place, it should be useful in its direct hint to the Boer belligerents that they do not real- ise the opinion of those who are looking on as to the uselessness of the prolongation of the war. This hint, coming from the Dutch Government, which alone among European Powers has accredit- ed the Boer delegates,mnst carry weight with the commandos who are showing at once so much pluck and so much foolish obstinacy.ln the second place, the Note from Holland is highly important in eliciting from our Government a plain declara- tion on the alternatives of a fight to the finish or a settlement. Lord LANSDOWNE, in his answer, clearly puts upon the B oers leaders in the field the onus of the choice. It is for them to say, he states, whether they desire a settlement. And to prove that he is sincere he adds that Lord KITCHENER has been instructed to forward im- mediately any offers he may receive. In other words, our Government is willing to give- fair con- sideration to any reasonable offer the belligerents are willing to make. With that avowal the hard and pernicious doctrine of requiring unconditional surrender goes by the boards. Whatever else our European critics may say against us, that charge can no longer be urged against us, and the stain of it is removed from the pages of history. Its continued assertion would have been the darkest blot in the tale of the war. There is also much to be said in favour of our Government's 4 view that it could not accept the proposal made by another Government avowedly 1 without knowledge whether this proposal was de- sired by the Boer delegates, and bearing in mind also that the Boer delegates themselves might in a remote contingency be repudiated and derided with ourselves as puppets lased in a movement on our part to get out of an embarrassing war. In all diplomacy there must be assurance as to the authority of the persons acting. Lord LANSDOWNE in whatever he did, would have to speak as the mouthpiece of the British Government, and our Government could not with dignity make even the first step in negotiations with sucn an uncertainty as this. Besides, it is reasonable that the win- ning side should expect the losing side to indicate when it thought that enough fighting had been done. So far the Ministerial reply should meet with approval. The point of differ ence will occur at the emphatic declaration that negotiations must take place in South Africa and not in Europe. That is the decision which Lord ROSEBERYA his sagacity has wished that our Government would avoid. Until the position of the Dutch delegates is clearly defined they cannot, as we have said, be considered. But:if the fighting Boers acknowledge the author- ity of the delegates, and are willing to add other responsible delegates to them, Lord ROSEBERY'S opinion must carry great force, and he doubtless advanced it with this qualification in his mind. The bitterness of feeling in South Africa is not con- ducive to peace. It would be an insult to the combatants to hold that they would not accept the terms of their leaders, whether acting in Europe or South Africa but their leaders would recognize the facts much better in Europe than in South Africa. Besides this we know that Lord Muzfna's hand in this matter would be certain to excite prejudice. To conduct the negotiations in Europe would not belittle Lord MILNER, and it would be in the natural course of proceedings, Mr. KRUGER and his remnant of authority having gathered at the Hague. In all business affairs it is well to avoid exciting unnecessary prejudice. Lord ROSEBERY'S suggestion met that difficulty, though he avoided mentioning it. Unfortunately, our diplomacy obliged the revelation, and this harsh sentence in
an otherwise adrairable Note may blight the hopes which the correspondence had raised

DOCTORS and sanitarians The Smallpox appear to be baffled by Epidemic. the advance of the smallpox epidemic in London. So, at least, the London newspapers affirm, and yet it is evident that -the most obvious precautions against the progress of the enemy are neglected. The optimism which has characterised the War Office in regard to the campaign in South Africa appears to have cast its baneful influence over that other Dephrtment, the Local Government Board. It seems a curious travesty on life that while the seeds of one of the most distressing and dangerous of diseases are being sown all over the metropolis, such an assembly of business men as the House of Commons should ignore the spread of the epidemic, and busy itself with the subject of how many questions shall be put to the Speaker before dinner, how many after, and whether it is nicer to have Wednesday evening off for social parties or to have a longer week-end in the country. As business men, the members of the House of Commons should be ready to cake the simple financial step on which both vaccine- tionists and anti-vaccinationists can agree, and that is to enable local authorities to enforce quar- antine regulations, supplying them with the means of compensating those affected for temporary loss of work. That course has been adopted at Leicester by the aid of a special local Act of Par- liament, and it appeals to common sense. It is easy to understand how, under present circum- stances, in a city which has been aptly described as a province of dwellings, the epidemic spreads; the most mysterious thing is that it has not deve- loped much more rapidly. A factory worker living with his father ansi mother and some four brothers and sisters is stricken. The symptoms, and even the outward evidences, of smallpox are so little known that for some days it is unsus- pected, and the contagion is distributed among the family. The young man is removed to a hospital, the sanitary authorities make an ostenta- tious display of drugs and cleansing liquids ; and meanwhile five people, some of whom have most probably caught the disease, are quietly allowed to carry it along as many lines—into shop,. office and factory—without any sort of precaution. To keep them from their work, when possibly they live from hand to mouth, would be very unfair, unless they were given compensation for they would be driven to receive from the Guardians or to go into the workhouse. It is, however, by this licence that an unsaen web of mischief is being spread over the metropolis, and the pattern is being steadily interlaced. The authori- ties have traced, for example, no fewer than seventy cases to one early case in Holborn. In another instance, through an error in diagnos- ing smallpox as chicken-pox, the mischief done is at present incalculable. The wife of a 'bus con- ductor sickened, the man tended her by night,and distributed tickets by day along three miles of the West End. That particular danger has at last been modified by the requirement Ulla all cases of chicken-pox shall be notified as infectious disease in the metropolis; but the distribution by people who have notoriously been in close con- tact with the actual sufferers from smallpox while the disease was beginning to manifest itself goes on without demur. How much more vigilant was Mr. WALTER Lorro, the Minister responsible, when, as president of the Board of Agriculture,he had to think about the dogs. His determination to stamp out rabies was marked by a remark- able courage and an indifference alike to the cries of dowagers, of dog breeders, of foreign importers and farmers, and of actresses- Every dog, although ha might be an aristocrat among dogs, had to suffer the severest of hard ships. In the present instance, to take the most obvious step for keeping down small-fox among human beings, all that is needed is a small ex.. penditure of money. If people were reimbursed for their loss of time they would, for the most part, cheerfully submit to a short period of en- forced leisure. As it is, however, we seem inclined to wait until the epidemic assumes alarming pro- portions,and then become energetic. The sarcastic remark made at the beginning of the South African war that it was all right—" we should muddle through successfully "—has its warning for many departments. A prosperous nation like Great Britain needs to shake itself to avoid vs inertia. We are too slow in our movements. Vigilance in seeing the approaching shadow and averting the evil, or limiting its course at the beginning, is far better than a fine amount of energy in combating it after it has gained possession of the citadel.

The slander case has ended as most people ex pected it would—in a verdict and damages for the plaintiff. Councillor F. R. Roberts had a strong case while that of Mr. Pemberton was correspond- ingly weak. in the first place there was no getting round the fact that a slander had been uttered, and attempts to justify slander usually end in failure. Neither Judge nor ' counsel favour such a method of defence even when a good case could possibly be made out. In this instance Mr Pemberton's attempt at justi- fication was a feeble one and we can only conclude that for once in a way he over-stepped legal bounds in his rash utterances at Parr Hall. The action will probably have a wholesome effect on the agitators who for so long have not hesitated to heap opprobriuM on the heads of individuals who have never been proved to deserve it. We thought we detected, at the meeting on Wednesday even- ing, a more cautious and temperate tone in the speeches which were delivered. Ono hundred pounds damages, with costs, have a wonderfully quietening effect

it Economist " upon the Remarks made by th more tolerant attitude of the extreme Temperance Party, will find an echo in tho mind of many Well-wisher of the temperance movement, in the provinces, who has often been amazed at the manner in which that section of the party has stood in the way of desirable legislative reform, for no bettter reason than that it did not go far enough. There are some of these, who would reject the whole of Mr Ritchie's proposals on the same ground. But the authority named, like very many others, is glad to notice the salu- tary change which enables the extreme ' section, and consequently the Temperance Party as a whole, to no longer insist upon having all or nothing, but rather to accept freely an instalment of what they hope to get bY and bye. It is such an unexpected attitude for these people to take up and one which Mr Ritchie has been well advised to make the most of. The extremists have too long played the part of the dog in Aesop's Fables, which, with a piece ot meat in his mouth while crossing a stream, and observ- ing what it conceived to be another dog having tt similar piece of meat, makes a grab and loses all. Even the "Times," which generally speaks of the teetotaler as being a " fanatic," calls Mr Ritchie'e a "modest measure which leaves untouched maul parts of the subject." Such measures generally' do, and to reject them entirely on that account 15 not only nawise, but is eminently calculated to raise and foster a suspicion that agitators weula •

nometimes rather agitate and make speeches than act, and so put an end, possibly, to the making of further speeches. Chambers of Commerce in England must by this time have arrived at the conclusion that there are many so-called business-men to be found wedded to the old ruts and ancient grooves as there are among the farmers. For years past some of these Chambers, scattered all over the country, have hammered away at the question of adopting the Metric System in relation to weights and measures, but have only realised hitherto that the British nature is such as enables it to take much preliminary work of this kind to prepare the way for any important change,be it ever so promising as regards its value. It is not very long since one of our most important Chambers of Commerce received a communication on the subject "with laughter." Yet there is at this moment an influential demand for legislation making the metric system compulsery, and at a recent meeting where a resolution to this effect was adopted, it was stated that the system was already used by four hundred and eighty-three million of civilised people, and that the British nation was simply achieving splendid isolation in this as in other respects. Still there are English people who think we have had enough of this iso- lation, and that it is high time for some of it to be ended. Possibly. the reader may be one of these.

The Chief Constable's report upon the state of crime in Warrington must give satisfaction to all law-abiding citizens. "I am pleased to report, once more," says the Chief Constable, "a marked absence of serious crime within the Borough." Considering the opprobrious epithets which are so freely given to Warrington, it is gratifying to have at first hand such a statement as that which the Chief Constable has made. We believe that Warrington will compare favourably with any busy manufacturing town in the country for immunity from serious crime, audit is a matter for congratulation that each year shows a marked improvement in this direction. An indirect evi- dence of the good conduct of Warrington people generally is aff.,rded- by a comparison of the numerical strength of the police force in Warring- ton and the average stret.gth of police forces in the Northern district of England. Whereas the aver- age in Warrington is in a proportion of one constable to every 931 of the population the average in the Northern District of England is one constable to every 68192 of the population, or in other words, the force in Warrington would have to be increased from 69 to 93 to coring it up to the strength of other forces in this part of the country. Fortunately thew is no need for such an accession of strength to the local police force.

div.head: FATAL RESULT oF AN ACCIDENT
div.p: FATAL RESULT oF AN ACCIDENT
AT RUNCORN.
A Singular Case. Inquest and Verdict.

Mr Robert Dobson, held an inquest at the !Runcorn Police Court on Saturday touching the death of Thomas Parker, who resided at 4, Malcolm-street, and whose death took place o Wednesday evening, Mr John Yates was foreman of tne jury. Mr Robiuson, of the firm of Messrs Oliver, Jones, Billson and Co., solicitors, Liver- pool, and Mr F J Norman, represented the United Alkali Co. Mr Erant, inspector of factories, was also present. Sarah Spruce, 4, Malcolm-street, wife of Henry Spruce, labourer, stated that deceased was her father, and he was 67 years of age. On Saturday, the 25th Inst., deceased came home from work, and said a rake had fallen on his foot. Ho did not say when the accident occurred. He eat down and witness took his clog off, and deceased's foot then became swollen. She could see a mark on the top of the foot, but the skin was not broken. Witness welt for Doctor Robinson, and he came to see the deceased a little after six. He attended deceased several times till his death on Wednesday evening at seven o'clock. Dr Robinson suggested a consultation, but no one was called in. John Benson, residing at 10, Surrey-street, and employed as a foreman at Wigg's works, stated that he knew to deceased. He was at work on Saturday, the 25th ult, until abut four o'clock. Deceased thee said he was going up to his tea, aril witness expected him to return. He did not come back to work. He had been working from six o'clock in the morning. He had not been off work that week, and he never mentioned the injury to hi] foot until the Saturday. Just before he Went home he had his clog and stocking off, and las said his foot was very sore. tie told witness he dropped a I rake on it at tee beginning of the week, hut he had not felt anything of it until then. At his request witness examined the foot, but could see no bruise or weund and it was [lot swollee. D,ceased was working at getting the cinders from the furnaces. The rake would be about 14 feet long, and had a flat head like a garden rake. It was of iron. Witness could not tell the weight of it. The deceased said he dropped the rake on his foot himself. Dr Robinson stated that he was called in to see the deceased on the previous S aturday evening and atten- ded him several times up to his death on Wednesday, the 29 tit January. He found the foot swollen and ten- der. Deceased told him that he dropped the rake upon , his foot early in that week. Witness could not remem- ber the day. He thought it was very remarkable that the man could work. He must have been a tougher raan than witness. He thought it was a likely case for , gangrene to supervene owing to the vitality being low.' The man developed fever and delirium, and he passed into a typhoid condition, The pulse became intermit- tent. There was no external wound, and witness could not discover any fracture. The crush was on the instep. , Witness incised the bruise, and recommended poultices. This treatment was calculated to preserve vitality in the injured part. The cause of death was septic fever resulting from inflammation which had been set up by the crush, the deceased being a person of old age, and of low vitality. The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the doctor's evidence.

We have been vquested by Mr F. J. Norman,manager. of the works, to state that deceased was a good work- man of some service, and he was respected by his employers, who very much regret his death. Had he reported the accident he would have received lEig. a week, and any extra nourishment which might have been required.

div.head: INQuAsTs AT RUNCORN.
div.p: INQuAsTs AT RUNCORN.

On Monday evening an inquest was held touch- ing the death of John Lamb. infant son of John Lamb, moulder, Ellestuere-street, Runcorn, before Mr J D 013,3013, coroner.—The evidence showed that the child had been treated for pneumonia by Dr Bethune and that on Saturday night the parents retired to rest with the deceased. In the morning it was quite dead.—A verdict in accordance with the medical evidence was returned.— An inquest was also held touching the death of Jane Faulkner, widow, Loch-street.— It appeared from the evidence that the deceased lived with her daughter. On Sunday night, the 2i3th January, Pncebe Faulkner,deceased's daughter who slept with her mother, was awakened by her crying As she got no better,medical assistance was sought but she died on Sunday last. The medical evidence showed that the woman bad had an apopletic seizure and a verdict in accordance with this evidence was returned.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES. . [BY A CORRESPONDENT.]
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES. . [BY A CORRESPONDENT.]

The business at the Council meeting on Thursday was of a purely routine character and does not call for any special comment. It was mentioned incidentally that the work of preparing for the erection of the transporter bridge was proceeding apace. The contractors and the manufacturers who have the matter in hand are busily preparing the ironwork &c, and ere long Runcoraians will see the structure uprear itself as the material arrives at its final destination. Another call has been made on ' Runcorn. as on other shareholders for a further installment of £l,OOO towards the total capital promised by the Council. This week the shareholders of the Runcorn Co- operative Society have been having quite a busy time of it. Every six months three of the members of the committee have to be elected for a term of two years. This year has witnessed no less than nine candidates for the three seats. Canvassing, a thing unknown in previous contests had been re- sorted to, and the result was a remarkably keen contest. People are naturally asking why there is such a keen desire to be on the "Stores Com- mittee "and at present there is no proper answer forthcoming.

The Petty Sessions on Monday was a very light affair indeed. Ttianks to the watchfulness of toe gentlemen in blue, crime seem i to be at vanTsoing point. There certainly was not enough business done last Monday to meet expensae which points to the morals of the town being exceptionally good.

INI ERESTING PRESENTATION ro MR. R. H. POSNETT.

On Thursday evening Mr It H Posnett and his wifegave a tea in Brunswick schoolroom,Runcorn, to the employees of the High&ld Tannery Com- pany and their friends in honour of the birth of a son and heir. Considerably over three hundred persons sat down to an excellent repast to which full justice was done. After tea a capital programme was submitted. Mr Posnett presided and he was supported by a number of influential ladies and gentlemen. Prior to the con- cert the event of the evening took place. Mr Green- halgh, in a few well chosen remarks explained that 'as a token of the esteem in which Mr Posnett was held he would draw his attention to a memento which had been subscribed for by the employees of the Highfield Tannery Company.—The presentation then took place, which consisted of a massive silver bowl made by Oldfield's, Liverpool, bearing the following inscription " Presented to R. Pogue% Esq., managing director of the High- field Tannery Company, Runcorn, and Mrs. Pos- nett, by the employes of the above firm, as a token of respect and esteem,and in commemoration of ,the birth of their son and heir with every good wish for their future welfare and happiness."—Mr Posnett suitably responded to his employes for their unex- pected present.—The concert was a thorough suc- cess, the efforts of Mr Mountfield (humorist), who had been specially engaged, being highly appre- ciated. Mr Cox had charge of the tea, and the room had been very prettily draped by Mr T Leach.

div.head: WIDNES AND RUNCORN BRIDGE COMPANY.
div.p: WIDNES AND RUNCORN BRIDGE COMPANY.

The report and balance sheet of this company was issued to the shareholders on Thursday. The directors state that during the year contracts for the erection of the bridge have been arranged, the foundation work being let to Messrs W fhorntoa and Sons of Liverpool and the superstructure to the Arrol's Bridge and Roof Company, Limited, both being contractors of the highest standing for work of this character. Although v(ry little change is to be Peen at present on the site of the work, a large portion of the contractors plant is on the site and good progresa has been made in the preliminary arrangements and in the construction of the bridge at their works. ,Mr L U Cease, ,vho has been appointed resident engineer, has taken an office at Runcorn near tbe work. It is expected the bridge will be completed about the middle of next year. The retiring directors are Sir John Branner, Bart., M.P. and Mr H Seton- Karr, M.P., both of whom are eligible and offer them- selves for re-election. The balance sheet Rho ws that the authrrised capital of the company is £lOO,OOO. all of which had been subscribed. £2 per share—£2o,ooo had been called up and another call of £l. per share is now made. The expenditure shows that the purchase of the Act of Parliament cost £lO,OOO, and Government duty on capital was £250. There had been paid engineers on account of fees £2,000, Manchester Ship Canal Company for purchase of land under section 18 of the Act, £l,OOO ; and to the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster. for grant of force lore and bed of river Mfrsey for site of bridge £lO5 Ms. The sum of £314 as 4d had been paid as interert on paid up capita,. The legal charge frr formation of company stationery,secre- tary and office expenses c sme to £4ll 9s 81 and adver- tising propectus, ern. totalled. £383 18; 81. div.head: PROPOSED HOSPITAL FOR EARLESTOWN.
div.p: THE PROPOSED HOSPITAL FOR EARLESTOWN.

A meeting of the General Committee in charge of the above scheme was held at the Town Hall, Earlestown on Tuesday evening. Mr T Ormand presided and there was a fair attendance. A report from the Ladies' Committee was submitted from which it appeared that they have, worked assidu- ously for some time past with the idea of holding a bazaar in order to raise funds for the scheme, and ' they have decided to hold an open air bazaar, due- ling July, and it is recommenced to hold a demon- stration and gala in connection with it. The question of support being accorded the scheme by the working men of the district was discussed, but the matter was held over until something definite was heard from the men at the Viaduct Works. The reorganization of the General Committee was intro- duced, and will be dealt with at the next meeting. NEWTON, EA.RLESTOWN AND:DISTRICT HORTICUL- TURAL SOCIETY.

_ The annual general meeting of this society was held in the Town Hall, New:lon, on Tuesday even- ing. Mr J Randall presided and he was supported by Messrs A Smith (hon. treasurer), 8 Randall (hon secretary), and other members of the society. The balance sheet was submitted from which it ap- peared that the receipts amounted to £73 2s 71 including the balance brought forward. £5 163 sd, subscriptions .£39, and gate receipts £lB 15s. The expenditure amounted to £64 93 51d, leaving a balance in hand of a 133 lid Mr Smith stated that since the balance sheen had been drafted a further sum or £1 3$ had been received for subscriptions and this would bring the 'balance up to £9 163 ID. He pointed out that the largely increased balance had not been obtained by decreasing the prize money but by re- ducing the expenditure in other directions. This year they paid for prizes £29 16s,against £2O 12s 61 the previous year. The committee was re-elected with the addition of Messrs W T Strange,Pierpoint, Ball and P Knight. The names of Messrs W Dalton, J W Thorpe and D Barry were added to the list of patrons. Mr A Smith was unanimously re-elected non treasurer and Mr S Randall, bon secretary. A vote of thanks was accorded to the donors of prizes. A sub-committee was appointed to revise the schedule and the proceedings terminated with a vote of thanks to the chairman. div.head: AT EARLESrOWN.
div.p: AT EARLESrOWN.

A conference of the members of the National Association of School Attendance Officers (War- rington district) was held in the Board room of the I Town Hall, Earlestown, on. Saturday afternoon. The objects of the association are, to im- prove the status of school attendance officers, to afford legal or other aid where necessary, to assist in the better and more effici- ent discharge of their dutieq, to encourage social intercourse among the officers, and generally to promote their interest and well-being, to obtain remuneration for their services commensurate with the importance of their work,to secure superannua- tion allowance when by reason of old age and in- firmity they were no longer capable of performing ,1 their duties. At the coaference there were present —Messrs W T Strange (Ashton), P Barnes (Leigh), W Bomber, II T Kane, W Jones, J H. Scsrisbrick, W Rutter (Warrington), 0 E Hoberts (Manchester;. 0 Davies and C Forster (Widnes), J Longvvorth (Bolton), T Bromelow (St. Helens), J J Brown (St. Helens), W Fasquill (Golborne), J Cooper (Farn- I worth near Bolton), and T Martindale (Earlestown). Instructive papers were read at the Conferance,and discussions took place upon them. At the Close, the members were entertained to tea in one of the lecture halls of the Town Hall, by Mr T Ormand, I chairman of the School Attendance Committee I (Newton). An excellent repast was served, which was thoroughly enjoyed.—Mr Roberts (Manchester) ' spoke at some length on the objects of the associa- tion.—Mr Jones, of Warrington, moved a vote of thanks to Mr Ormand for his hospitality.—Mr Cooper (Farnworth), seconded and it was carried with heartiness.

Sr. PETER'S DAN' SCHOOLS, NEWTON.

The annual entertainment promoted by the officials of St Peter's schools took place in the Town Hall, Newton, on Saturday and Monday evenings As on former occasions the greatest care had been bestowed on the training of the children, and as a consequence there was a very large audience who thoroughly enjoyed the treat !provided for them. The first part of the entertainment consisted of Items by the junior scholars, and comprised the school song " Village bells " ; dialogue ; musical drill; action song, "The tall top hat," and the dialogue, 'Three litLle mothers." All these items were exceptionally well given, and were thoroughly enjoyed by those present. The second part of the evening's entertainment consisted of the operetta "By the Ganges Banks." This was a Hindoo representation, and according to the argu- ment, Lieutenant Rodney, a British naval officer, visits a remote part of India on the banks of the Ganges. The people of this district are worshippers of Vishnu, whose high-priestess Akela, bitterly resents the ever-increasing British power. She vents her spite on Myrrha, the Lieutenant's promised bride, and would have brought about her death had not Rodney arrived with timely assistance. The characters were : Myrrha (a Hindoo Princess), Annie Rose; Akela (High Priestess of Vishnu), Sarah Blything I Newasi (a Hindoo maiden) Annie Leather; Kitchena (Myrrha's servant) Harry Ly9ns ; Lieutenant Frank Rodney, W Pearson; Ben Brace (Rodney's servant) John Webster; Mowgli (Chief Fakir) Arthur Davies. In addition there were Hindoo women and Hindoo men and Fakirs. and British sailors. The dresses I were capitally designed, and the acting and singing of the children graceful and tuneful. Mr Singleton and his assistants deserve the highest praise for the excellent way in which the piece was produced, and the rapturous applause was sufficient evidence of the enjoyment created.

div.head: NEWTON URBAN DISI RIOT COUNCIL.
div.p: NEWTON URBAN DISI RIOT COUNCIL.
The Lighting of the District.

Mr W Coßingwood presided over the monthly meeting or the Newton Urban Dietrict Council which was 13(11 at the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Monday evening. There were also present :—Messrs C B F Barron, J W Emmet:, E T Evans, W Gilmour, T Orrnand,N Siddeley, J Simpson, Dr Patterson and Dr Latiaam witu A Bowes (Surveyor) and C Cole (Clerk.) MR. GILMOUR AND TBE LIGHTING OF THE DIS fRICT. STRONG COM PLAIN r.

At a meeting of the Use Co:nmittee a letter was read from the Clerk o the Golborne Urban District Council in reply to the letter from this Coat cil, stating that he had been instructed by the Lighting Committee to inform this Council that they are unable to take the matt,... of lighting of Rot-lane in hand at the present time. A letter was read from the Vulcan F.Jundry, Limited, stating that, as they contemplated cicsMg their gas works, they would be glad to know whether the Council could supply all their requirements, which would be about 6 to 7 million cubic feet per annum. The letter from the Sankey Sugar Company, applying for a supply of gas for their works and other propeny which was submitted to the meeting of the Gas Com- mittee held on the 21st October, 1901, was again read. , the estimated amount of gas required being about 3 million cubic feet per annum. It was resolved that the Sankey Sugar Company be informed that the Coun- cil will grant their request, on the terms and conditions to be hereafter agreed upon and that the question as to whether the Council are able to supply the requirements of the Vulcan Foundry, Limited, be deferred until the next meeting, to enable the Gas Manager to report as to the production of gas at the Gas Works.

Mr Tnompson movn-d the adoption of the minutes, Mr Gilmour made a strong complaint with referenco to the gas supply in the district. A gentleman told him that on Friday night the lights kept " jumping " and they were sometimes almost in utter darkness. Another authority had given him an estimate with regard to lighting, and this showed that Esrlestown and Newton wort two of the worst places in England for the supply of gas. _ .
Mr Thompson said Mr Gilmour's remarks had no reterence to the minutes,
Mr Gilmour : Jr is no Use pssQing accounts when we have gas that we cannot see and read by. The minutes were apprtmed. WATER COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of this committee tile report of the sub- committee appointed to consider the application of the Sankey Sugar Co. for a supply of water to their cot- tages and other property (but not their works) in Earlestown, was read, and it was resolved that the Sankey Sugar Co. be informed that the Council will endeavour to supply them with the water required for theirleottages and their other property, other than the works, as soon as possible. The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr Borron seconded by Dr Patterson.

div.head: AN 0 BJEC CIONAB LE FENCE.
div.p: AN 0 BJEC CIONAB LE FENCE.

The Highways Committee resolved that the Clerk be instructed to give notice to Mr A C Leslie (Lord Newton's Agent) to remove the fence which had Dee n erected on the Ashton-road,and that if the work be not carried out within seven days from the date of the notice the Surveyor he directed to have the fence re- moved.

_ On the recommendation of the representatives of Town Hall Ward it was resolved that the three new streets off Common-road be named : —Ponkford-street, Short-street and Brook-street. A letter was read from the Local Government Board, approving of the re-appointment of Mr Elenry Asticeoft as Inspector of Nuisances for this district for one year from the 24th January instant. —lt was resolved that the Medical Officer of Health be instructed to report to the next meeting of this Committee as to tae adoption of volun- tary notification of phthisis. Mr Thompson objected to the adoption of the minutes referring to the passing of the plans for houbes sub- mitted by Messrs Finning and Wa,gg on the ground that they were not in accordance with the byelaws. He pointed out that a month ago some plans were referred back because they were not in accordance with the byelaws but these plans had been passed notwithstand- ing the fact that they did not conform. Mr. Gilmour supported the objection and said he did not wish to " make fish of one and flesh of another." The Surveyor said the plans infringed a byelaw which had never been enforced in this district, the one which required all new buildines, dwelling-houses particularly, to have the parting wail carried through the slates to a certain height. Mr. Orinand asked if it were reasonable that at'ention should be drawn to this matter, when the Surveyor tzld them that the byelaw had never been enforced. He was afraid that those who would refer the matter back to the committee were actaated by a spirit of peevishness. Both Messrs. Thempson and Gilmour strongly denied that they were prompted by this spirit. _ . . . . .

Mr. Emmett asked if it would not be adviqable either to amend the byelaws or give notice to all builders that they would be enforced. Mr. Barron supported the committee's recommend- ation as the requirements whicq had been mentioned by the Surveyor waa quite obsolete. Th 3 minute; were ultimately approved. GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of this committee a letter was read from Messrs Peace end Ellis (solicitors) stating that they had been informed by the solicitors to the Smith Lancashire Tramways Company, that the Company have already entered into contracts for the construction of tramways running from Haydock throuzh Ashton, Abram to Hinciley, from Hindley to Hindley Green, Atherton to Bolton, from Atherton to 'fvldesley, and from Atherton through Leigh, to the boundaries of the Borough of Leigh and Leigh Rural, and that the Company da not propose to commence any works in Newton or Galtiorne until these tramways are finished.—A letter was real from the Clerk to the Guardians of the Warrington Union, giving notice of the intention of the Guardians to discontinue the use of the office at the Town Hall in March nest.—A letter was read from the Rev J Ryder, informing the Council that the clock, which has been placed in the St. Peter's Church tower, is now comp let' and asking the Council to make arrangements for the winding and keepinz in repair of the clock, and for incandescent burners to be used for its lighting. SUPERANNUATION BILL.

The Finance Committee resolved that the Council be recommended to approve (under their Common Seel) of the principles of the Local Authorities Officers' Adop- tive Superannuation Bill, 1902, to enable Local Authori- ties to provide for the superannuation of their officers and servants, and do hereby revest that the name of this Authority may be included in Schedule II of the ' Bill, as Authority to which the Act shall apply. The Council agreed to tills course. This was all the businesg.

div.head: PROPOSED Y.M.O A. AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: PROPOSED Y.M.O A. AT EARLESTOWN.

A meeting for the purpose of tatting into consideration, the formation of a branch for Earlestown and district of the Y.M.C.A., was held in the Town Ball, Earlestown on Monday evening. There was a very large attend- ance, over which Mr Thomas Molyneux presided, amongst those present being the Revs T R Matthews, E C Becock, Dr Latham and Mr E J George. Mr A K Yam), representing the Y.U.C.A., and National Council delivered an address in which he set forth at. some length the aims and objects and advant- ages at such an association. At its conclusion, ' The Chairman propesed that a branch of the AssociA- tion be formed in Etriofitown. _ . _

Mr W H Dale seconded, and it was unanimously carried. Mr Duncalfe moved" that we hereby constitute our- a elves the Earlestown Branch of the Y.M.C. A., accept- ing the Paris basis as our guide." Mr Wheatley said he understood there were two classes of membership. Mr Yapp said members were Christian men, associates might be Christian men, or they might not, but the I latter cuuld not hold office or yore. Mr Francis seconded the motion which was carried. Mr Yapp said they would need to appoint s secretary, and it should be understood that all the officers they appointed that evening should be appointed pro tent. As soon as possible they should have a more general meet- ing,to which they would invite all the Christian men of the town,and then they could choose the best men they I could got to act on the committee, and as office bearers. Mr Platt, of St. Halens, was appointed secretary pro tern.

The following were appointed a provisional commit- tee : —Messrs T Molyneux, W Pierpoint, A Francis, T Parr, D McHardy, W H Dale, J Gee, 3 Harrison, H Pearson, Joseph Webster, A King,T E Clough,W speak- man, Clarey, and Dr Latham. With regard t, the rules, Mr Yapp said the genera plan was Co adopt en bloc the rules recommended by the National Council, but they could amend them to suit their local requirements. The rules were adopted provisionally. On the motion of Mr Molyneux, seconded by the Rev. T R Matthews a vote of thanks. was cordially passed to Mr Tapp. Mr Yapp said the best way to apply that vote of thanks was to put their backs into the work, and make it a success. He was more convinced every day of the necessity of getting hold of the young men. The Associa- tion might be of untold good to the whole of the dis- trict if the men who were present that night put their whole heart in the work, and he trusted it would be tremendous success. (Hear, bear). Mr Clary of St Helens also spoke in support of the Association. _
------ A voto of thanks to the Chairman terminated the meeting.

div.head: LOVELY LANE.

Alderman SUTTON proposea the acceptance of the minutes of the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee. Wuncillor BENNETT Ee 3ond ad ani took exception to the resolution in regard to toe wv'euing of Lovely-lane to 40 feet. He thought that width inadequate and suggested that the lens be 50 feet instead of 40 feet. He moved that the minute be referred back.

A discussion followed, Alderman Sutton saying that there was no alternative but to pass the resolu- tion as it was in accordance with the bye-laws. If they widened the road any further they would have to pay for the land required, whereas they were getting :,he present improvement ror nothing. Councillor JAliiNs EVANS seconaed the amend- ment.

Csuncillor PLIMIPTONT said he was anxious that the roa 1 should be wider but the terms offered by Lord Newton's agent were so good that they could not see their way to do anything but accept them. The DEPUTY MAYOR proposed the approval of the minutes of the Museum and Library Committee. He said he was sure the Council would pardon him in alluding to the loss the Committee had sustained of one of its oldest, m 1,4 respected and useful members, the late Mr John Peers. (Hear, near.) He was an unostentatious man. and for 27 years he had been one of the honorary curators of the mveam and library, and he had done very valuable service. It was due to his memory that this public testimony should be paid to his work. (Rear, hear.) Councillor GREENING seconded, and confirmed what had been said about Mr Peers. Personally he felt his loss very keenly, and he was sure every member of that chamber would rec )gnize the good work the deceased gentleman had done. (Rear, hear). The minutes were approved of. AN EMBRYO CENILTERY SCANDA.L. In seconding the adoption of the minutes of the Cemetery Committee, proposed by Councillor JoHrr EVANS, Councillor JAMES EVANS alluded to a tale that had been brought to him about some person being found in the cemetery in a dying condition and not receiving proper. attention.—Councillor John Evans satisfactorily explained. The man was taken into Mr Young's house. afterwards seat to a doctor and finally taken home.—Councillor Baird : Every attention was paid to the man. —The minutes were passed. TEIE GS OFFICES. _

Alderman FA-IR-O-LO-U-G-H- proposed toe adoption of the minutes of tee Gas Uommittee, and alluded to the plans for the alteration of the gas offices in Nlersey-street, and the extension at Ltudgford. The first was necessitated by the Tramways Committee taking part of the old office; down, and a new coke shed was wanted at Longford. It would save labour and expense. Alderman BOLTON seconded. Alderman Snsw GREEN: Row does the Gas Committee propose to pay for this? AlderTaati FAIRCLOUGH : Out of capital if we Can get it. Alderman SHAW GREEN said it was usual to ask the permission of the Local Government Board or pay the expenses out of revenue. Councillor JAMES EVANS suggested that before spending this money they snould consider the ' question of the concentration of all the offices of toe Corporation Councillor BuziNETT ohjectA to the money be- ing paid out of revenue in the present condition of the rates. The committee ought to borrow the money in the ordinary way. Councillor Pirecocx proposed an amendment that the resolution in regard to the gas offices be omitted.—Councillor WrizaNsorr seconded. Councillor PLuNIPTONI : What will it cost ? Alderman FAIRCLOUGH: About .CBOll at Mersey- street. We are going to build a lock-up shop which will let for nearly as much as it costs. He believed they could pay for it out of capital. Only font voted for the amendment and the minutes were confirmed. FIR[ ENGINE COMSIITrEE.

Councillor SMETHURST mentioned that the damage done by tire in the town and district dur- ing the past year amounted to £36,ooo.—Councillor Plumpton seconded the propositiou that the minutcs I be passed and it was carried.
WATER CONINIITTEE-RAPID RISE IN SALARIES PROPOSED AND REJECTED.

Councillor JoHN EVANS proposed the adoption of the minutes of the Water Committee, which recom- mended that the salary of Mr George Mitchell,chief aseistant engineer, be increased from £156 to £,175 per annum, and the salary of Mr Neil Mc K Barron resident engineer, from £156 to £175 per annum. He said that Mr Mitchell had been engaged on the, new reservoirs at Winwick and Appleton and had supervised the work in a highly satisfactory manner. Mr Barron was temporarily engaged in the preparation of the plans and quantities and his work had also been very satisfactory. Mr Barron had also been appointed resident engineer at wick at a salary of .C1.56,in place of a man who had been discharged. Councillor BAIRD seconded.

Councillor SMETHURST objected to the increases. He said that both the gentleman concerned started in 1900, Mr Mitchell at £lO9 4s and Mr Barron at £93 12s. They must be clever people, for in addi- tion to being raised to £156 each, it was now pro- posed to give them £175. In two years they were raised from about £lOO to £175. He proposed that the minute be referred back and the salaries of the two gentlemen mentioned reconsidered. Alderman BOLTON seconded, and said he was not satisfied that these gentlemen were worth the money they were offering them. A little re-organisation was required in the offices of the Water Committee. One gentleman received a gratuity because it was not poss- ible to raise his salary until February. Two or three years ago the committee made £2,000 profit per annum. They were now making £5OO, aad in a year or two he expcted they would have to raise a fund to meet expenses. The DEPUTY MAYOR said it was only fair to state with regard to the loss oi profit that Alderman Bolton's alma- (lions were entirely' outside the mark. The difference in Iprofits was in consequence of the repayment of principal and iute7est on part of the loans incurred on capital expenditure. It Was most unfair to draw the herring in that way. He also pointed out that they bad no expert professional assistance to pay for—the work had all been done by the staff. It was not intended to ktep these gentlemen permanently..... Councillor JOHN EVANS : Mr Mitchell is a permanent official.

Couxeillor TINNION referred to the irregularity men- tioned in the payment of Borne official, and thought an explanation would be wise. With regard to Mr Mitchell, why had he not been put upon the sliding scale adopted In ether departments of tue Corporation? A maximum should be fixed. _ . .

Councillor —IOIIN EVANS replied and slid that Mr Barren was not a permanent official. The irregularity was this, when Mr Mitchell Wats appointed permanently it was just past the time for asking for an increased salary. Be was very heavily engaged in preparing plans and quantities and engaged up to all hours of the

/night. It was thought only fair to recompense him for this overtime and the matter was explained to Althrman Bolton at the time and he agreed to it. 'Phis gratuity of £5O was paid to Mr Mitchell in sums of £5. It was really a payment for overtime. A vote was then token and Councillor Smethurst's amendment was carried by II votes to 8 votes. The minutes were then confirmed with the exception of the oae relating to salaries which was referred back. A " PRO-TEM " MANAGERSHIP.

IThe DEPUTY MAYOR proposed the minutes of the Tramways Committee, and chew attention to • the arrrangement to have the name " W H Grimed&le, manager " painted on the tram cars. As he stated at the last meeting Mr Grimsdale was manager ppo tent, but the Board of Trade required that whether temporary or permanent the manager's name should be painted ea toe tram cars. He sincerely hoped Mr Grimsdale's work would not necessitate any change in the name. [hey expected to start toe cars in a few weeks. (Hear, hear). Alderman BOLTON thnt referred te the negotiations between this Committee and another for the valuation of some land and property, and said the Borough Sur— veyor had to be called in to settle the dispute. He merely added the two valuations toe her and divided by two. (Laughter.) The DEPUTY-MAYOR: Alderman Thilton is in a state of chronic inaccuracy. There is a difference of about £l.OOO in the two valuations, ana without calling in the Borou2ll Surveyor they tuemselves took the course mentioned.

Alderman BOLTON • The Borough Sarveyor said so. The DEPUTY-MAYOR : Well he was pulling your leg then. and It shows the (xtreme innocence of your nature t) accept of the statement as true. (Laugetcr.) The , cost of the valuations did not reach £2O. In reply to Alderman Botrx‘r, toe TOWN CLERK said the bye-laws and regulations for the tramcars were modelled on those of other towns. Tao minutes were passed. THE CORONATION CELEBRATIONS.

WARRINGTON BRIDGE WIDENING POSTPONED. The MAYOR proposed the adoption of the minutes of the General Purposes Committee, and alluding to the Coronation said he was sure it would be the sincerest wish of all that the celebrations should be worthy of the County Borough of Warrington and of their loyalty and devotion to their King and Queen. More than that be could not say except that the matter had Inen lett with the Parliamentary Committee. The DEPUTY-MAYOR seconded.
Councillor Bass/Err said be thought they had done themselves credit by shelving the memorial to the Queen.

Councillor PLumproN alluded to the resolution" That no further steps be taken for the proposed widening of the bridge until the tramway sys t.eno toas been in work for at least six months," and that if it read that the delay should be until there was a coroner's inquest it would be more. in harmony with the possibilities. (Hear, hear.) Why should the improvement be held back six month,when everyone present knew how dangerous the bridge would be? Councillor Piumpton then drew a fanciful picture of what might happen to a nurse-girl and perambulator crossing the bridge. There was al- most certain to be an accident. He could not see any reason for delay. Everyone was agreed that the Canti- lever scheme was now in a practical form, and it was only those gentlemen who were determined to spend £20,000 or £30.000 on a new bridge who were delaying the present scheme. (Hear, hear.) • He thought they were doing an injustice to the people who used the fridge by delaying the improvement. He proposed as an amendment that the Cantilever scheme be proceeded. with without further delay. COUUCHIOr SMETHURST seconded the amendment. Tnere would be somt ole killed, be was certain, unless the bridge was widened.

The Maros said the and water pipes caused the delay. Tiaey ought not to hurry such things too quickly. The TOWN CLERK then read the following letter from the consulting engineer, Mr J Webster :—Dear Sir,—l have received your Istt ar of the 27th inst,with enclosurea from Mr Haddock and Mr fleas. The object!on raised by Mr Deas to the pipes being too near the surface was one of the strongest objections raised by me when.l sent in the plans ; and it was partly owing to this objection that I proposed the arched ribs. As you are aware, I was not at all in favour of the plans for the cantilevers, on account of the many objections :which I have already pointed out, and I was very much astounded to see it reported Ithat one of the members of the Council had stated at a meeting that it was "my own child." I simply worked to instructions, and made the best of a scheme which I had strongly condemned in my report. The proposal to carry the water and gas pipes as shown on the drawing prepared by Mr Dees is quite impracticable ; the structure would not carry its own weight, and if the cantilevers are to be as shown, they would have to be considerably deeper to extend much further back into the masonry, which brings us back to the old trouble of cutting into the arch stones. If the bridge is to be made still more unsightly by placing the pipes outside. , the only satisfactory plan is to lower the cantilevers and I ongitudinal girders, and support the footway and the pipes as shown on the drawing which I enclose here- with. If the pipes are to be carried outside as shown, the cantilevers will have to be strengthened consider- ably, and this will of course increase the cost propor- tionately. I need hardly say that I still consider the arched ribs,either;for the widening or for a new structure to be the most satisfactory method of dealing with the structure. If a new bridge were constructed, I think I pointed out to you that the old structure would remain, until one half the new work was erected; and the traffic would be then transferred Co the new portion until the second half was completed. Yours faithfully,—Joss J. WEBSTER.
The Mayon : I thick it would be better to defer for one reason or another the alteration of the bridge for some time.

Councillor TIN 5105 said they were on the same game as before. There was a dei e riming tion in some qaarters that they would not have this cantilever bridge at any price. He thought it was only fair that having fought the matter fairly and the new bridge scheme defeated, the present scheme should be put in hand at once. He understood that the difficulty of the pipes bad been overcome. He did not know whether Mr Webster was asked to raise difficulties, but he wished he would settle some of them. (Hear, hear.) He saw no sufficient reason for the delay. In answer to Councillor Plutnpton, the Tows CLERIC said the Borough Surveyor's report to the General Purposes Committee was sent to Mr Webster for his further consideration. Councillor Tisslos : It has been well worked. After some remarks by Alderman BOLTON, who opposed the delay, A vote was taken and the minutes were canfirna by - -
15 votes to 10 for the amendment. A discussion of the resolutions re municipal trading followed. and a report of the speeches w ill be found in another part of this paper.

div.head: SLANDER AT PARR HALL
div.p: SLANDER AT PARR HALL
Action at Manchester Assizes.

Roberts V. Pemberton. £lOO Damages. Severe Comments by the Judge. The much-talked of slander action brought by . Councillor F R Roberts, solicitor, Warrington, , against Mr John Pemberton, builder, Stockton Heath, has been heard. It occupied the attention , of Justice Wills and a special jary in the Nisi Prius Court at Manchester Assizes on Monday and Tuesday. The verdict was judgment for the , plaintiff who NV9.9 awarded £lOO damages It was alleged by the plaintiff that the slander was uttered ; by the defendant at a meeting held in connection with the Municipal Non-Trading Committee in the 1 Parr Hall, on December 16th. Mr Sties, K C , and Mr Byrne, instructed by Mr T H Dootson, of Leigh, appeared for the plaintiff, and the defendant was represented by Mr Taylor, X C., and Mr Langdoo, instructed by M-ssre Spencer Wellhead and Son, Of. Lyme-street, Warrington. ' Considerable local interest was taken in the action ' and on both dabs of toe hearing of the case, many Warrington faces were to be seen in the Court Room. Amongst other interested spectators Was Mr Norbury It was nearly 3 30 un Monday afternoon ere the case was reachen. OPENING STATEMENT BY COUNSEL. Mr Shee then rose to make his opening state- ! ment. The plaintiff, he pointed out, was a gentle- man carrying on his profession as a solicitor in Warrington. lie was a Master of Arts, a Bachelor of Law, a member of the Victoria University, and an Associate of Owens °allege. He was also a member of the Warrington Town Council. The plaintiff, although he practisee as a nelicitor, occasionally preached at the Wesleyan Churches ! - in Warrington, and on one occasion in December he delivered a sermon at, the Wesleyan Chapel ! Sankey Bridges,on behalf of a friend, Mr Brough9 I who was unable to take the duty that day. There- ! upon the defendant, ln the course of one of his political addresses to his constituents in Warring- ! ton, went out of his way to make a violent and ( cruel attack upon the plaintiff in his professional ! eapa city. It was o meeting which had been well i billed an I which attracted an audience of some , 4000 oersone. Shortly stated, the substance of the groundless accusation made against the plaintiff I was to the effect that he bad betrayel his client. ' a poor man, who had had a small claim male against him by some creditor living outside War- rington, by anvising him, contrary to his client's interests, to sign a deed of assignment, when there was no need of it, when the client was well able to carry on, business an Is that he had done this in his own interests and in the interests ' of nis brother. The slanderous part of the defendant's speech read as follows 'Councillor Penny Roberts,in that beautiful sermoa which he gave, referred tonharity. It brings back to my mind a very paintul incident. It is a thing I ' shall never forget white I live. Tier° was a man in Virarringtoa who was a tenant of mine. He W 1.3 an honest man, and he start-d in business for him- self. He had vvorked hard, and had got a nice little I business about him, and was doing very well indeed That man was pressed by a person outside the town who did not know him, and he sent him a latter saying than if he did not pay a certain ! amount within a certain time he would put him in the court. He had ample money in his business to pay that small accounnbut he could not gat it in.A% it was urgenthe went to Councillor F it Roberts for advice. He owed his (Councillor Roberts') brother through the Slate Company, an account. Council- lor Roberts asked him to come next morning and bring his papers with him. When he went next morning the brother was there, and he told him ' that the only thing he could do was to have his affairs straightened up—in fact, to sign a deed of I assignment. That same morning—it was a strange I thing—he had to meet me with reference to his I rant, which was eighteen months behind. I hat perfect faith in him. I just simply wanted to know when le could pay it. I could see that the man was so upset that he did not know what to say. I asked him what his position was, and he told me eventually. I went to Mr Fred Roberts after he to'd me, and I asked him to allow that man to go on, as I was quite certain we would get our money if we gave him time. But no, he would not, I threatened to seize certain things on the property, as 1 had a right to do as landlord if be was pressed. He said I could not do that. I replied, I will show you whether I can or not. I shall sell all the stuff" Re eairl."You dare not lay a finger upon it. It will cost you more than the estate will brio e you." I said, " If you allow this man to go on he will pay both you and me. I will no:, take a pennyworth It was no We. He was sold up, and from that day to this, nearly two years ago, that man has walked about unable to do any ' work, entirely through the effect on his nervous system which that bankruptcy brought about. This is the man who dares to talk about charity!" There was no doubt, continued Mr Shea. about the meaning of all this. It accused Mr Roberts in his professional capacity of having induced his client, when he could still go on, to sign a deed of assign- ment in the intereste of himself and of his brother. to whom the poor man Morris owed a debt. The statements in the defendant's speech Were certainly altogether untrue. The facts of the case were that this poor man ',Morris was a man who at one time bad been employed by the Warrington Slate Com- pany,with wbi !,h Mr Roberts' brother W 49 connected —he believed as a director. Morris was employel as a foreman carter, and he after- wards set up in business for himself. It was his praciica te buy coal from this slate company and sell it again. He used also to Cart coke from the Warrington Corporation Gas Works. He made no profit on the coke, but made money on the mir- age. Against this man the plaintiff entertained no ill-feeling of any sort. Us once or twice acted for him professionally, and was, indeed, kindly dis- posed towards him, and was anaioua to do the very best for him. In regard to the p aticular allega- tions made by the defendant, the true facts were altogether at variance with his statement. In 1897—a year before the date of the assign- ment alluded to in the defendant's address— Morris had a claim of £7 10e made against him by a man named Hart, of Liverpool, in respect of a surety which Morris bad entered into on behalf of a man named Macdonald:Morris pei 1 the money to Hart, but was desirous of being refunded by Macdonald. He consulted Mr Roberts about inane the plaintiff, haying gone thoroughly into the matter, found that there was no doubt about Morris's title to have the money recovered from Macdonald. As it wan however, a case in which proceedings would have to be taken in Liver- pool, Mr ,Roberti very properly advised , Morris to place the matter in the hen is of a Liverpeol solicitor. Marisl;onsented,and plaintiff communicated with Mr Kelly, a Liverpool solicitor, asking him to do what he could for Morris. There could be no doubt whatever, ceunsel pointed out, that that claim on Morris by a creditor from outside Warrinnten was ie1897. and it was all done and finished with in September of that year. So much observed counsel,for the statement that Morris was being psessed bv an outside creditor for a small sum:in 1898. In 1898,what'nempened was that Morris had got into serious difficulties with his business, and he owed money right and left, some £350 altogether. He calculated his assets at £253, but many of the articles put down as assets were after- wards found to be doubtful, and the £253 assets were reduced by about £5O. Subsequently they realised only £139. Teat was the financfal position of Mr Morris in 1898. He was very much distressed and tried to do what he could to carry on his busi- ness. Ile tried to borrow money from his friends but without success, and he had no ready cash with which to meet any of his debts. He was being pressed at his bank as well as by his creditors, and he was in a state of despair when he called once more on Mr Roberts for advice. So anxious was he about the matter that he went to see Mr Roberts at his private house on Sunday. Notwithstanding the fact that the call was made on a Sunday, Air Roberts went fully into the matter with Morris, who admitted that he could not possibly raise any money. Mr Roberts explained the alternatives, bankruptcY included, but both agreed that this was only the final alternative, as Morris Was anxious to continue his business, though on a smaller scale. Ultimately, Mr Roberts said there was nothing for it but to draw up a deed of astignmennand this was a course which the plaintiff honestly believed to be the best in Morris's interest, and action was taken accord- ingly. It was, said counsel in conclusion, mon- strous to suggest that this advice shocked Morris or had had any detrimental effect on hie health, He thought the jury would know how to deal with

a man who, whilst talking politics, went out of his way to attack another person in his private and prolessional capacity in the presence of two or three thousand people, who were likely to carry away most of the mud and dirt that was flung. TILE JUDGE AND THE WARRINGTON PRESS.

Frank Fennelly then read kis short-hand notes of the statement made by Mr Pemberton in Parr Hall. tirrl'aylor : Perhaps you can tell me what the allusion to the " man from Manchester" means? Witness: It refers to Mr Norbury Williams, who has been interesting himself in Warrington affairs in connection with the trading by members ot the Council with the Corporation. In further cross-examination, witness stated that there were about 2,000 people present at the meet- ing. On reference being made to the Warrington newspapers containing the report of the meeting in Parr Hall, it was pointed out that toe partie.ular passage in Mr Pemberton's speech, alleged to be slanderous, had not appeared in the local news- papers. All the reporters left it out. Mr Justice Wills: Quite wisely, I think. (Laughter). THE PLAINTIFF IN TUB BOX.

Frederick Richard Roberts, the plaintiff, then entered the witness box. Having stated his degrees,he said that for some time he was a Congre- gational minister. He decided to leave the ministry and took honours in the final. He had carried on the profession of a solicitor in Warrington since 1891. Sometimes when his (pladatiff's) friends had been unable to conduct services he had preached far teem. In Dacember,prior to the occasion on which defendant made the speech he complaine i of he preached for a frieni, Mr Brough. He did not attend the meeting at which the speech was made. 'He had known Morris about 25 years. Up to the year 1891 Morris was employed in some capacity by the Warrington Slate C3mpan3. In thet year he left and set up business for himself He hal acted once or twice professionally in some little matter for Mr Morris. In September. 1897, Morris came to him to ask him about a sum for which he had been surety and had had co pay. He gave Morris advice, and entered the advice in his diary,which he had with him now. Morris had been surety for a Mr Macdonald, and Macdonald failing him he had to pay £7 10s. Morris came to see if he could recover from Mac- donald. He (plaintiff) told him that he could if Macdonald was good for the money. He (Morris) instructed him to write and he did so ou September Ist. He had no answer whatever. Mr Morris and his wife came to see him about it frequently. As a result,. on September 14th, he (plaintiff) said that as the matter as likely to be an action in the Liverpool County Court, Morris had better put it in the hands of a Liverpool solicitor. He agreei to that. Ile (plaintiff) wrote a Liverpool solicitor with the papers on the matter and instructed him to proceed. The levers were copied in his diary. Ile read the ia- struction. Teat had nothing in the world to do with the deed of assignment executed in 1898. So far as hertplaintiff) had aaything to do with it that was the only outside claim ho (Morris) had against him. That was twelve months before. Consulting his diary plaintiff Weilt on to say that Morris came to his house at eleven o'clock in the morning of Sunday August 14th. He (plaintiff) told him that he did not care to transact business as a rule on Sunday,but Morris was in such mental distress that he consented to see him and talk matters over with him. It:was a beautiful summer's day and he took him oe the lawn. They sat there and were in conversation between one and two hours Morris wishe Ito see him about the state of his aff airs. He told witness that he was depend- ing for his supply of goods upon two companies one of which was te Slate Campany, who supplied him (Morris) with coal. The other was the War- rington Corporation Gas Department, who supplied him with coke. Morris told him he was three months in arrears with his payments to the Slate Company, and that they had stopped him and would not supply him with any more goode on credit. He also Old him that he had bad a letter a few days before from the Gas Department of the Corporation demanding payment of an accoant of .£76 by return of post, and saying that all future transactions must be on the original basis. What traubled Morris most of all was the pressure the landlords were putting upon him to pay arrears of rent and he had n 3 means whatever of paying them. He kplaintiff) could not under- stand how it was that the landlords had not put in their distress until Morris painted out that he had also borrowed money from the landlords and on inspection of certain receipts it was quite clear the, the money which he had been regularly ov- ine f w rent had either with or without his know- ledge been credited to his loan account, and increasing the arrears of rant and thus preserving the power of distress. He went into the whole of Morris's affairs. He showed him a list of his creditors from which he gathered that he owed something like .£350, £4l of which was for arrears of rent. lie went with him into the state of his assets and tonne he had practically no money at all. His account was overdrawn at the bank land they demanded payment. He also found that he had only about £3O in his b3oks, and it was very doubtful from his own statement whether that ..£3O would be realized, because the debtors were simply people who owed him a few shillings for begs of coal and coke. Besides that he had nothing but some furniture (a portion of which was claimed by tie wife) three carts and three horses. He owed accounts of .£B7, £76, £4l, £52 and £2l. The debtor we.s well aware of his position. He (plaintiff) first of all questioned him about the possibility of raising any money to make some offer to his croditors of at all events some portion of their debts. He said he hed tried all his friends but it was of no avail. Witness 'old him it was useless to make any cash offer to his creditors, and it seemed to be also use- less to sad lie himself with the promise to pay them even a cemposiciou of any extent. He gathered that he was losing money in his business and itwas useless for him to make a promise to pay lOs or 53 in the pound. He was al-,o certain that in the state of his health and his business it was not right he should attempt to carry such a burden. He could not pay the old debts with the declining busi- ness and at the same time find money for goods he would want. It seemed to him that any attempt to get cash or to make a promise of cash payments was quite useless. He pointed out that there were two or three courses open to him. First of all there was bankrupcy. Morris was exceedingly anxious if possible to carry on his busi- nes.s on a smeller scale. Witness pointed out that though bankruptcy would relieve him of his debts, it would mean one or two very serious things, In the first peace, unless he paid 103 in the it was very likely the Official Receiver would oppose the granting of a certificate, and tnerefore his discharge might be suspended and he might be prohibited from carrying on business for two, three, or five years. Mr Shee : You say might. Is it not the usual thing? Plaintiff said it was, Morris could not pay Furthermore Morris was in a delicate state ces health. His eyesight had been failing for some timer Witness told him he would have a very unpleasan public examination to undergo. Mr Shea : Was the furniture part of the assets? Witness said it appeared that the larger part of the furniture was claimed by Mrs Morris. He pointed out that such a claim as that would be most vigorously investigated by the Official Receiver and probably the claim might fail. That was anether reason he advised him against bankruptcy. Mr Stare: Was there an asset put down for a shed. Plaintiff said there was and Mr Morris valued it at £lO. The landlords claimed that as a fixture attached to the freehold and got it. The question of a bill of sale was mentionel. Morris could not , find any money, and the question arose as to whether he (:sittings) could. He pointed out that no man would lend' money on a bill of sale where , the landlords had the power of distress for £4]. hanging over him. The thing was absurd. There , was no security. Having talked all these things . over, he urged Morris to execute a deed of assign- ment tor the benefit of all his creditors. Witness , told him he thought he would have considerable . influence with two or three of the largest creditors certainly with one, and that he could get them to agree to the deed. The inducements he held out to him to show him the advisability of execut- ing a deed were these. In the first place he pointed out that it was a great thing to get a friendly trustee; that a friendly trustee under the powers of the deed would be able to agree to any claim they might make and give it good title behind which no creditor could get. He told him that if he got a friendly trustee who would come to witness for advice he (Morris) was much more likely to get his wife's claim admitted , than if he went to the Official Receiver. Mr Shee : You thought the deed of assignment was the best thing to do. Plaintiff ; When Morris saw his way

His Lordship pointed out that there was the interview with the defendant. Plaintiff said the defendant came to see him four daye after tee deed. The deed was executed on the Moadey. Defendant came on the Thursday, with the co-landlord (Mr. Mainwaring). The real reason of the visit was that they had put in a distress. Defendant said he had. They had come to see tem about it. Defendant's case was that in August, 1898, Morris was in need of cash, that he was not insolvent, but that, if his position had been duly inquired into, and that if he could have got time and been able to induce his friends to lend blue a helping hand, he would have got through and been able to carry on his business.
