Warrington. People's Cc:liege Infant School Children's Concert.

The above concert ;Thics.rk—w—ai given on Monday evening proved itself to b 3 a decided success. The attendance was excellent, the schoolroom being filled to its utmost capacity,and many paople were unable to obtain admi4sion. Mr Edward Walling- ton made a short introductory speech.Misa Walling- ton and her staff of teachers deserve the highest praise for the results obtaine I by their patient and skilful teaching It seemed hardly credible that such wee children could be taught to do any- thing so worhy of public opprohatiou,as that done on this occanion. The items on the pro- I gramme were numerous but those most deserving of mention included en action song entitled " Railway trains," tha driver and guard both perfcrming their duties in a first.rate manner. The babies of the school did their best in a recita- tion entitled " Ten tittle servants." Eva Newell Sang "Slumber Dolly,' the chorus" Lullaby" being sung by all the babied. The drills were well con- ducted the boys making their mark in their per- formance of the "FlagAwe love," whilst the tambourine drill by the Oirle proved to be their best effort. Apay n —3ach (a bonny wee girl) appeared dressed a 3 a fashionable lady " making calls." She so invited her to repeat the same, ple,;sed the audience with her " call " tahnadt y graciously complied. A good recitation was gives by Bessie Barlow 1 the lie lad and Harry Kay. entitled " Dirty Boy." Dur- ing the eveninv Misq Wallington, in a short speech, said she wished to thank averyoue for their kind attendance. She wets sorry they had been so crushed, but that should be remedied at the nest concert. She explained that the first object of the concert was to raise money with which to buy pictures to adorn the walls of the schoolroom, and apparatus for use in the teaching of some of the lessons. Another object wps to show the parents what their children were taught in these very commodious and well-fittel schoolrooms. She thanked all parents for their kind assistance in the dressing of the children for that evening's en'er- tainment. a:l4
MR. HARRY BERREY'S CONCERT AT WARRINGTON.

The small audience that assembledin Bold-street Wesleyan Schoolroom on Thursday last week enjoy- ed a musical treat.:The programme was provided by the St Helens Male Voice Choir and the members of Mr Harry Berney's Opera Company. It is diffi- cult to account for such a small audience unless it is that the Warrington public has beco Le satiated with concerts owing to the large number which have been provided in the town during the season. Male VJice Choirs have been much in evidence owing to the formation of two such choirs in the town, but the record behind the St Helens choir which delighted all who heard it on Thursday, is one of which any choir may well be proud. The choir contributed five items to the pro-. ' gramme and all were given in a manner that gained the hearty approval of the audience, The swieg and balance of the parts left little to be desired ; if anything, the second tenors were a trifle weak and the basses correspondingly too pro- nounced. The prettiest p.ece of the evening was undoubtedly' Watch her nindly stars,'' given with- out accompaniment,whilst for robustness and clear 1 expression "The Crusaders " must claim special mention. Mr Berrey conducted with marked ability and acknowledged the appreciation which the audience freely bestowed. A slight indis- position prevented him from doing himself justice as a soloist and his interpret.ition of " Mona was not equal to Mr Berrey's previous performances in the town. He was more successful in the duet " Tenor and baritone we are respectively," in which he was joined by Mr R Atherton. The effect produced by the blending of the two voices was excellent and called forth a well-deserved en- core. "The Toreador" was the title of Mr Alfred James's song and he gave an effective rendering of it. Mr Willie Milne in his humorous songs was a favourite with the audience, despite the fact that he was handicapped by a relaxed throat, He also took part in the "Sobbing Quartette," in which he was accompanied by .Vises Berrey and Dennett and Mr Berrey. This was one of the most amusing pieces of the evening, and the audience could not resist the temptation to ask for "more," and the re- quest was responded to. All the artistes acquit ted teemselves well, but the palm must be given to Mr Milne, whose inimitable mimicry delighted the audience. In the operatic choruses the voices of the members of the male choir were blended with five female voices. Solos and choruses were given from the " Geisha," " Mikado" and "Bohemian Girl "in a manner which reflected credit on all concerned. Mention must also be made of the song and chorus ''The Merriest fellows are we ':from the' Gondoliers," in which the male members of the opera company were very success- ful. Miss Berney proved herself a capable leading soprano and distinguished herself in the choruses. Miss Dennett's mellow contralto voice; was heard to great advantage in the solo "The Swallow," the trills being pleasingly interpreted. In response to an encore she complied with the song " When Jack and I were Children," Miss Ethel Parr was only fairly successful in her interpretation of" The Flight of Ages" and the same remark applies to Miss Greenough's interpretation of " A Japanese Love song." Miss Richards took tee leading part in the miserere scene in "Ii Trovatore.' The duties of acconopanist were discharged with taste and skill by Mrs Berrey. A CLEVER PICKPOCKET AND A PHENOMENAL LIAR.

On Friday morning the msgistrates at the Warrington Police Court beard a somewhat extraordinary case. A girl named Clara Jones, aged thirteen years and resid- ing in Pierpoint-strer t, appeared in the dock on three charges—first of stealing from the person of Florence Morris in Bewsey-road on the afternoon of Januery 15, a purse containing Si. secood,of stealing from the p rson I of Elizabeth Ann Vernon at 830 p.m. on January 18th a purse containing is sil, and third of stealing from the person of Charlotte Houghton on January 29th a puree containing 5s 70.—She pleaded guilty..—The Chief Constable said that for their worship's purposes only three charges were preferred against the girl which was the usual limit in police court cases, although he could have brought as many as eight or ten charges against her of a similar nature. In the first case Florence Morris resided at 5 Albert-etreet and at one o'clock on January 15th she was in Bo wsey-road. When cresting Bewsey Bridge she saw the prisoner who at that time was unknown to her. Tim eirl commenced to talk with her, nib being her usual custom when she was about to plunder the pecket of her victim. She walked along with Miss Morris for some diftance, and when Miss Morris went home she missed her purse. Remembering that the prisoner had been with her, she found out who the girt was and went to see her mother, who returned her 2s and the purse. Ha (the Chief Constable) should like to say at the outset that the girl made a statement that she had from time to time given her mother money and purses the proceeds of the thefts which she had comrnittectand the woman had received them with the full knowledge and understanding that they were stolen. That, of course, the woman denied and there was evidenes per contra that ou at least two occrsiens she had returned the Stolen purses and either the whole or part of the money. There was no corroboration of either the girl's or the mother's statement Under the Juvenile Offenders' Act the bench had the power if during the hearing of the case it appeared to them that the mother was responsible or in any way answerable for the girl's crime, to order I a remand and have the woman brought before them on a specific charge at the next hearing. In the second 1 ' case Elizabeth Ann Vi rnonotho reeided at 96 Catherine. street, was passing along Wiwsey-road on her way home at 8 30 p m on January 18th accompanied by her moi her I and saw the prisoner, who came close to her. At that time Mrs Vernnn had a purse in her pocket containing is sfd,and she subsequectly missed it. The girl again fell ' under suspicion and Mrs Vernon went to see her. She at first denied having committed the theft but later on camel ,to Mrs Vernon's heuse and gave her the purse, which I was concealed in her clothing. There was nine/deuce left in it,and the prisoner said she had spent the remain- der of the money. The third case was of a similar I ria'ure. Mrs Boughton threatened to call the police, and in a few minutes Mrs Jones returned a Dime containing I 53 sed. In this case, however, the purse interned _did not belong to Mrs Houghton. They bed evidently got mixed in the purses. for this one turned out to be the subject of a fourth robbery. The stolen puree was sub- sequently found down a grid close to the prisoner's home. Information having been given to the police, Superin- tendent Moneenan arrested the prisoner. Bee des b ire a most expert little thief the girl wan a phenomenal liar and the police had not le?en able to place muchl reliance an anytbing she said. Prisoner said she had been nicking pockets for weeks and he (the Chief Con- stable) had a list of twelve cases which had been re- ported during the past few months from the immediate neighbourhood.—Mrs. Jane e was called and sail she returned two of the stolen purse.. When the first theft was committed the girl's father thrashed her and threatened to call in the police if she did such a thine again, but this was of no avail. Witness did not give any information to the police. She had only received one shilling from the eirl and prisoner paid she had found that in the market. —The prisoner was ques- tioned by the magistrates and said the gave her mother sums of 5s and 2s on separate occasions, the money having been stolen from people in the market. Her mother knew where she had got it from.—The maeis- trates decided to send prisoner to a reformatory for five years. The chairman (Mr Hopherd) addressing Mrs Jones said the Bench thought she ought really to have le,en in the dock as well and she had just escaped being sent to prison far a ensldorable time.

div.head: MUNICIPAL TRADING.
div.p: MUNICIPAL TRADING.
Discussion in the Couneil

At the monthly meeting of the Town Council held on Tuesday evening at the Town Hall under the presid- ency of the Mayor (Mr. J. Charlton Parr), there was a larger attendance than usual of the public, and it was evident that considerable interest was being taken in the motion to be submitted by Councillors Pierpoint and James Evans with reference to municipal trading. The meeting of the Council was probably the longest on record. It commenced at six, and the ordinary business, the motions standing in the name of Coun- cillors William Pierpoint and James Evans, together with one or two special meetings to pass certain reso- lutions, took up more than three hours. Councillor Pierpoint's resolution read as follows : "In order to allay the public feeling which has arisen with regard to municipal trading, this Council resolves that 4 com- mittee of investigation be appointed, with powers to make a complete and exhaustive examination of all the books, papers and documents of the Warrington Corporation extending over a period of the past five years ; and that such commi itee be authorized to call to its assistance such members of the Corporation, officials and others as in its opinion maybe necessary to facilitate in any way the desired inquiry : provided the cost of such inquiry be paid by the Warrington Municipal Non-Trading Association ; and this Council further resolves that the committee of investigation consist of four neembers of this Council, together with two representatives of the Municipal Non-Trading

Association." Councillor PIERPOINV said he would not venture to take up the time of the Council very long that night— (hear, hear)—because it was in the memory of all of them that a month ago he made a certain statements and certain arguments were used for and against the principle of a public inquiry with reference to alleged illegal trading between members of the Council and the Corporation. He commenced his motion by stating that" In order to allay the public feeling, this Council resolves that a committee of investigation be appointed." No one could deny that in Warrington , there was a very strongfeelingwith reference to the sub- ject of his motion, and it was in order that they might get rid of that feeling that he had ventured to place his motion on the agenda paper. He stated a month ago that that feeling was not only prevalent in Warrington. In all parts of the country where he visited the fair name of Warrington was used in a manner that was not altogether satisfactory to him. Therefore if that was the case he thought it was perhaps only right to say that it must be doing Warrington a great deal of harm because it could not possibly be doing any good. (Hear, hear.) The public feeling had itself in a variety of ways. They had ha'd sermons for the inquiry and they had had sermons against it. (Laugh- ter.) Unfortunately libel actions had arisen out of the question and there had been a correspondence in the public press, which to his mind had not reflected very great credit on some members of the Corporation. Statements were made a month ago by a certain Alder- man in that Chamber which, to Ids mind, did bear the impress of truth, but, after reading the correspondence which appeared in the public press, he could come to no other conclusion than that it was the Alderman's deliberate design to mislead him and other members.of the Council with reference to this publie inquiry. The question lay between the public and the Alderman, and he left the matter at that point. Now he agreed that a public inquiry was necessary and, of course,that was the crux of the whole question—whether the Council would be agreed as to the necessity for a public inquiry or not. He was not quite certain' but the Council might depend upon one thing, that while he stated an inquiry was necessary it should be of the fullest character. (Hear, hear.) They might depend upon it that before the discussion was finished the Council would find such a difference of opinion with reference to the form that inquiry should take, that after all, he was afraid they would not emerge into the light of day, but, perhaps, go into a deeper fog than they were at present.—At all events that was a question for the Council to deter- mine. If they thought an inquiry ought to be held let it be as full and as free as possible—(hear, hear)—be- cause he as a member of the Council must take his share of the onus of the charges laid against the Coun- cil as a whole. He would like an opportunity to be given to the detractors of his good name to show whether he or other members had been guilty of conduct that was not fitting for a member of the Council to be guilty of,or letthem (the other side)here- after hold their peace. He was strongly of opinion that this agitation was much exaggerated—(hear.hear)—and he was also strongly of opinion that if the Council gave an opportunity for an inquiry it would be found that the agitation was altogether unfounded. (Hear, hear.) He believed that it was stated in the motion that was to follow his that specific charges must be made. He had no hesitation in saying that he could make specific charges against members of the Corporation. He was also prepared to say that he was not going to make them. (Laughter.) Let other people mako them. Let them take the responsibility of makingrhem. He knew what the charges consisted of, and he wanted to give the people making them an opportunity of find ing them out for themselves.ille was prepared to go to that extent, to give the fullest and freest oppor- tunity of examining everything which would tend to elucidate any difficulty that might exist in the minds of these people (the Municipal Non-Trading Committee). And one means was by placing the motion which stood in his name on the agenda paper. The one thing that had interested him more than another was with reference to the form of inquiry, he meant the committee that should have charge of the inquiry. Members of the Council would, perhaps, I not agree with him but he offered to introduce along with four of their own body two members from the opposite camp. It was only fair that these gentlemen should have an opportunity of sitting with them and helping them to-try the case. The members of the Muni- cipal Non-Trading Association might possibly think they were not given a sufficient influence on the committee inasmuch as he proposed four members of the Council against two members of their own. He did so on these grounds—that the inquiry would of necessity have some disorganizing effect upon parts of the Corporation work clerical work,upon which the charges might have to be formulated. If they had a preponderating influence of Councillors on the committee they would assure themselves that the disorganization, temporary it might be, should be lessened as much as possible and they would do that in the interests of the Council' at large. He had no personal feeling in the matter. His only object was to try to get the Council to do what he thought was best in the interests of the town. Let them get rid of the agitation. As far as he was con- cerned after that night he should never raise his finger in this direction again. Councillor PEACOCK seconded, and said he did so as one who had been charged with illegal trading in the town, and also to give the public the fullest and the hest inquiry they could have. He hoped the Council would see their way to pass the mction which Coun- cillor Pierpnint had just submitted. Councillor BENNETT said that at the last meeting he had the privilege of seconding Mr Pierpoint's motion, hut be could not see his way clear to doing the same that night. Instead he wished to move an amendment. Several members: You cant; et. Councillor TINNION : I have just been asking the Town Clerk the question. The TOWN LER : It is for rr against. Councillor BENNETT I think my proposal is much better than either of the others. (Lauehter.) Alderman ROBERTS thought it would be better if the two resolutions were taken together, bcc Inge they wanted to compare one with the other. Councillor Pierpoint wanted an exhaustive examination by four members of the Council and two representatives of the Municipal Non-Trading Association. He did not know why it should make any difference whether there was a preponderance ef councillors or otherwise,as each would know what the other knew and it would make no differ- ence as to the report. Councillor Pierpoint's resolution was simply that there he an inquiry to see If they could find out if anything had been done wrong. He did not see anything had about that. If there bad been any v.roug-doing the sooner it was found out tne better. They wanted this thing ended. They (the Council) Were satisfied they were honest. The other resolution said specific charges must be made. Before they could do that they muot find out what was a specific charge. EOUBCMOr JAIIES EVANS : May I ask which resolution is being discussed ? The Maxon: Mr Pierpoint's, I suppose. Alderman BOLTON : I was going to show you which is best. (Laughter.) The alaroa : There is only one before us. Alderman BOLTON : Are you going to pass them both. The MAYOR . There is only one before U 3. I am told that one cannot be put as an amendment to the other, and that the first must be dispo6ed of befote the second can come up. Councillor PIERPOINT : (Hear hear.) Alderman BounN I am rather in a fog with so many motions. (Laughter.) Councillor Preeporvir pointed out that his was a separ- ate motion altogether. Alderman BOLTON said he could not see that there Could be any objection to doing what had been done before. Councillor Tinnion's sub-commiteee held an inquiry into certain matters and were satisfied, and he could not sea how the Municipal Non-Trading Commit- tee could get anything more, and if that was the Case what was the use of squabbling ? But if tbere was something to come to the light, let them have it. Per- sonally he should vote for Councillor Pierpoint's motion. Councillor BENNETT said tie agreed with the greater part of Councillnr Pierpoirit's motion. Be was in favour of making the inquiry as sweeping and as comprehen- sive as possible. Hs did not think their friends outside would accept any thing else. He was sick and weary of the agitation. Personally he did not think there was Much to find out, and he honestly believed the agitation was based to a large extent upon what he stated at the

div.head: EXAMINER. FRIDAY FEBRUARY 7, 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER. FRIDAY FEBRUARY 7, 1902

last meeting—a very flimsy foundation, If the investi- gation would establish that fact the reputation of the Council would be vindicated. Be objected to the con- stitution of the tribunal on two grounds. In tbe first place he did not think it was not fair tea the Municipal Non-Trading Association that the representation of the Council should be in a majority and have four repre- sentatives to their two. In the second place the inquiry would be conducted with greater success and greater efficacy if in the hands of independent and impartial persons. The members of the Council were too much interested, and they would be the better able to get at a fair and honest conclusion if they had an independent tribunal more on the lines suggested by Councillor Evans, whose pro- posal he thought was a very sensible one indeed. That would be as satisfactory a tribunal as they could select. Be did not agree with Couocillor Pierpoint's proposal as to the cost. If, as he believed, the association were in I the wrong or had exaggerated these charges, it was I perfectly Air and right that they should bear the ex- penses, but if they were in the right, it was, of course, only fair that the Corporation should bear the cast. His proposition was that the question of paying the ex- penee should be left to the tribunal itself. The MAYOR pointed out that Councillor Bennett was contrasting the two resolutions, which he thought was hardly in order. They could not move one as an amend- ment to the other. They must each be considered in their merits. Councillor BENNETT said it seemed awkward if they were to be tied to the particular wording of a resolution and could not alter it, because nobody's language was perfect in this very unideal sort of world. It seemed to him many heads were better than one and by collabora- ting they could easily improve the resolution. Councillor WILLIAM ROBERTS said althe had to say was that simply so far as he was personally concerned he courted the fullest inquiry, and if he was proved guilty of any offence he would resign his seat the same day. Be had kept very quiet over the controversy up to now because he thought that perhaps others bearing the same name had said sufficient without his taking any part in it. But in his humble judgment, as one who had taken some little part in the town's affairs during his lifetime, the agitation was one of the moss cruel and unjust movements that had ever heen inau- gurated in Warrington—(hear, hear)—and what he felt more than anything else was that it was hardly fair to be expected to make any concession to this Municipal Non-trading Association because they had condemned the whole Council without allowing the slightest opportunity for any explanation whatever. (Hear, hear.) When he came on that Council he hoped that he came there with a lgood character. He had striven to do his duty in the I town, but his name had been held up as one of the black sheep. He defied any man to prove that his hands had been stained with the slightest impropriety since he had been on the Council. Councillor WILKINSON : Is this in order. Mr Mayor? We are discussing whether an inquiry shall be held. Councillor W ROBERTS : Yes, it is in order. Councillor WILKINSON : I don't care to have my time wasted like this. I do not think it is in order. The MAYOR : It is getting a little outside. Councillor W ROXERT3 : Very well, I will cut it short. What I have to say is that these men have pro. flounced judgment upon the case. Then why should they be part of the tribunal to prove it when they have already given judgment? That is all. Alderman MONKS said three questions occurred to him,' which if they were definitely answered would help somel of them to come to a conclusion. The fleet war bad Councillor Pierpoint in his negotiations with the other side any idea as to whether they were likely to accept his resolution or net ? The second was as to the ques- tion of cost, including oayment to officials of the Cor- poration wiles° time would be largely absorbed, and whom it was as little as they could do to see that they were paid tor overtime. The third was : had the Cor- peration any funds from which they could legally pay any expense in connection with such inquiry ? Councillor PIERPOINT, in reply, said he did not know whether he could be said to have entered into negotia- tions in the fullest sense of the word with the Municipal Non-Trading Association, but he was prepared to say that his motion if passed by the Council would be satis- factory to the Municipal Non-Trading Association. (Hear, hear). With reference to troubling the officials of the Corporation he thought that seeing the rate at which they had multiplied the number of officials of late years, it would be a very nice thing if they found them a little extra work to do As for paying them he would not think of it for a-moment. The two departments that would be mostly disturbed were those of the Borough Treasurer and the Town Clerk, and in these depastments they paid nearly £3,000 a year so that out of these handsome salaries the officials could very well spare a little overtime. With reference to what funds the Corporation might have to cover the cost of an in- quiry of that kind he could only say that, judging by the statements made from time to time by the Chairman of the Finance Committee, the Corporation was verging upon bankruptcy, therefore, he did not think that there were any funds to spare for an inquiry ; and be should like to assure them that the Municipal Non-Trading Association were quite prepared to pay the cost of such iequiry. He did not see how the question of using the funds of the Corporation could possibly arise. The DEPUTY-MAYOR : Is Mr Councillor Pierpoint prepared to act as one of the Council's four represents- tires in the inquiry and to give some of his valuable time to the elucidation of this important question ? Councillor PIERPOINT : I am, but I would rather not. The DRPUTY-MAYOR : And I know you won't. Councillor Tuesiore said he was exceedingly sorry that th 3 motions could not be amended* He mentioned the matter to Councillor Pierpoint some thine ago and told him he was certainly in faveur Of an inquiry provided such lequiry would be satisfactory both to the members of the Council and to the ratepayere. He hoped that Councillor Pierpoint would have submitted his resolu- tion to him ald be half promised to do so. (Councillor Pierpoint : Yes, I did). The two of them might have got a better one. He did not like either of the motions, yet he must either take one or none. Be was in favour of an inquiry, but he must know what sort of an inquiry it was to be. In Ceuncillor Pierpoint's motion it said an " exhaustive examination "which was to his mind hardly an inquiry. A. committee consisting of Councillor Hulse, Councillor Forshew and himself taadiheld an inquiry, the results of which were on record. Did they want anything more, (" No," and laughter.) He said seriously and honestly, they had had that inquiry. What were they going to:do with it ? What were they going to do the same with the proposed inquiry—pass it by, go home and shake hands with themselvse. He would not be a party to any other enquiry. If he was asked to serve upon any other enquiry he should say no. They had produced the results of their inquiry, and they had laid them before the Council. In that they bad the honest opinions and honest judgment of these three gentle- men and they could not get behina them. Be took it that the documents were there from which they formed their judgment. Did they think he was going to be a party to another such farce as that. This resolution of Councillor Pierpoint's was a very lame,poor affair. He could not congratnlate Councillor Pierpoint upon it. He simply said an "exhaustive examination," I and did not provide for any report. It seemed to him that they would be saying something like this to them- selves, "We will have a look through these books. If we tied anything we will make a row. If we find I nothing we will say nothir g." (Leughter).:lt seemed to be a sort of paving the way to see if there was anything to bold an inqiiiry about afterwards. (Hear, hear), Let them have an inquiry that would satisfy all parties. He was not going to quarrel with the Non-Trading Committee but he was not going to do anything that he did not think would be fair to both perties. Let them have an inquiry that would be above suspicion at anyrate—(hear, hear)—aa iespiiry say by a gentleman eminent in the legal pro- fession, but let the charges be specified. The charges could be as wide as they liked against any particular committee, against the contracts of any particular firm in' Warrington, or, with all due respect to one firm, the traesactions ot the Warrington Slate Company might be the basis of the inquiry it they liked; but they must know the basis it was to go upon. Ha was not going to give his consent to an exhaustive examination which would give certain gentlemen what they would con- sider a let of information that could be used in a certain way. It must be used in such a way as ta settle this agitation and satisfy the ratepayers and the members ot that Corporation. He was only sorry that Coun- cillor Pierneint's resolution did not cover the ground. I Councillor PIERPOINT : I have finished with it after te-night. Councillor DUL.E suggested that the tnetions might be deferred for a fresh one to be drawn up. There were good suggestions in both which ought to ba em- bodied in one comprehensive resolution. (Hear, bear.) Councillor RonEtte : I object to teat. I sha'l sup- port Councillor Pierpoint. We have been told times out of number we have nothing to fear. Why withheld Ellie inquiry ? Let us settle it at once and choke every- body off. (Hear, hear.) Councillor PLIMPTON said he intended to vote for Councillor Pierpoint's resolution. Councillor Tinnion said they had already had an inquiry. Tney all knew how that was curtailed. It was simply an inquiry with reference to certain bills the auditors refused to pass. Out of the three gentlemen who sat on that Committee two of them at least were in favour of further inquiry. Councillor Pierp lint had already said that an inquiry in accordance with his motion would satisfy tne Non- Trading Committee, and he had promised to sit as a representative of the Corporation, If they could per- suade Councillor Hulse and- Councillor Forshaw and someone else to sit with him, they would get out of the difficulty. Councillor A J JOLLEY said it seemed to him to be not altogether a questionlin which they ought to talk about small details, but of the broad Issue was an inquiry justified ? He strongly maintained that no such inquiry was required in any way or shape. Be would say this, however, even though he held personally that any inquiry was unnecessary, if any considerable body of the ratepayers of the town—of the intelligent ratepayers of the town—(hear, hear, and laughter)—wished for an enquiry, be would support it because as a democrat he

could do nothing else. But no such demand had yet been put forward. ("Oh " and hear, hear). Definite charges had) been made but they all fell under two heads. Some of the members of the Corporation had been accused of illegal conduct, all of them had been accused of immoral conduct. Were the peaple who made these charges of illegal conduct honest in what they said ? Did they mean it ? The thing lay in a nutshell. If any member ef that Corporation had been guilty of illegal conduct the law provided a remedy by which he could be dealt with and imposed penalties, and further provided that the person who secured a conviction against a Councillor should have half the penalty inflicted by a Court of Summary Jurisdiction. Had any action been taken to secure those penalties? No. What had prevented them doing that? Was it that they had not looked for evidence ? Some of them had been over and over again to the Borough Treasurer's and Town Clerk's offices and wasted the officials' time in searching for information they had been unable to get. Councillor Pieneornir : Which they could not find. Coencillor A. J JOLLEY : Which they could not find. That is what I mean, If that was so, Mr Jolley pro- ceeded, he asked if they had not been seeking for in- formation they could not find simply because there I was no snch information they thought they could get ? When they found that out did they cotes making these charges? No. They bad repeated them although they knew them to be absolutely baseless and unjustifiable. What restrained these people from taking the offending members into a Court of Law? Was it magnanimity? No, He did not think so. These people had brought these charges and sullied the fair name of that Corporation for many months past, and they went further and accused the members of immoral conduct. He had shown them that the first charge was false ; what importance could they attach to the second charge ? Were they the people to make and judge ethical charges of that kind ? They did not withdraw the fieeic charges but repeated them. He felt very strongly and very keenly indeed that from the very begieniag this agitation, the leaders of the agitstion,had ben tainted with the fatal vices of egotism and insincerP•e and that the whole movement was little better than an organised hypoc- risy. (Hear, bear.) Ought they to make any conces- sion to people who gct up such a movement ? He said no. and would contieue to say no. Be had a strong hatred of cant in any form. Councillor Pierpoint had asked what answer could they give to their critics. The best answer was to go on as they had in the past, quietly, fearlessly, conscientiously doing their doty, (Hear, hear.) , The MAYOR at this stage said :It is not my intention to intervene or to interfere in the controversy between I the Council and the Municipal Non-grading Ceminittee The matters in dispute occurred, if they occurred at all, long before I WB3 asked to take the office of Mayor of the Borough, and therefore I can have no knowledpe of them other than hearsay. My opinion would there- fore be valueless, but I may say that I cannot help thinking there has been much exaggeration and much personal feeling imparted into the matter which had much better have been left out. An inquiry to g 3 back as suggested five years would entail much expense and much expenditure of time and trouble on the Corporation officials and if moaey has been spent too lavishly and through channels which might be open to adverse criticism no enquiry can bring it back,but would throw good money after bad ; this is a matter Ido not wish to give an opinion about, but leave it as I said before in , the hands of the ratepayers and the Council. What to my mind is of more importance to the rate- payers and the town generally is this, that at the pre- sent time and since I have been acquainted with municipal affairs I feel I can safely say that nothing illegal, in fact nothing but what is honest and straight- forward has occurred in any of the Corporation Com- mittees which I have attended. I have now had nearly three months experience of municipal business and have attended more or less frequently all the committees except two, Museum and Gymnasium Committees, and I can say confidently that every committee meeting I have attended has been conducted in an honest,straight- forward and businesslike manner with due regard for the interests of the borough and without fear or favour to any firm or any individual and if any members of the Ratepayers Association would wish to have any as- surance on these points I sisal( be happy to give it them. Concluding I would say that if an inquiry is to be held by all means let it be held at once: The agitation is doing injury to the fair fame and good name of our town and if it is to be prolonged indefinitely will go far to make our Coronation year a year of discord and strife and enmity instead of what we all hope and wish te see it a year of harmony and concord, of congratulation and general rejoicing. With th-se few remarks I leave the matter in the hands of the Council. A long discussion followed and ultimately the motion, as well as'that standing in the name of Councillor James Evans, was rejected.

here had been too much sitting calmly. (Laughter 1 and hear, hear.) He had been attacked in this con- troversy and he had not sat calmly. (Hear, hear.) He could only say that if he had been branded in the pre- sence of 2,000 or more of his cheering fellow townsmen _

with having traded illegally and immorally with the Corporation of his native town, he would if he were innocent,spend his last shilling in fighting the man who 80 charged him and in repelling so odious an insinuation

(Loud cheers). THE RESOLUTION.—A NEW LINE OF ACTION. Mr ALFRED Hi:71.1%m proposed the folio wmg resolution: "That inasmuch as it is perfectly plain that the Corpora- tion will not have any inquiry whatever, it is hereby resolved that the Municipal Non-Trading Committee make every effort to elect ttie borough auditors and to elect disinterested councillors and also to bring the sub- ject before the Elousa of Commons." The Chairman,tie
said. had referred to a correspondence he had had in the . . -

_ . local papers with Alderman Shaw Green. Re thought they had nearly all read that correapondende and he thought they would agree with him that after it Alder- man Shaw Green could be aptly described in Euclid's definition as superficies—(laughter)—something that had length and breadth but not thickness—something which bad been crushed quite fiat. (Loud laughter). The speech of Aldarinan Shaw Green in the Council Chamber on January 7th was honeycombedwith
inaccuracied. Alderman Shaw Green referred to the ZlllahCompany and what Mr Norbury Williams saidabout ic, and pointed out that the secretary of the Municipal . .
Non-tra-ding Association wrote to th; newspapers clear- ing the accuracy of one of the_charßes made by Mr

Norbury Williams. All that Mr Fleming did was to write stating that Mr Nerhury Williams had made what was simply a clerical error in deecribiag Alderman Roberts as a directbr 'instead of a shareholder of the Zillah Company. Teen Alderm re Shaw Green intro- duced Buckley and Company. That was most unfortun- ate for they had forgotten about that Cempany. They ' were under the impression that the new charity had its inception when Ingram's was started, (Laughter) But it seemed it went back ten years further and started with Buckley and Company. They were obliged to him for the reminder. (Laughter.) Alderman Shaw Green also referred to the objectionable cause for the letting of Parr Hall and pointed out that the favoured Billpoeting and Advertising Company gave the Corporation a quid pro quo by giving them half the receipts for toe billpesting. What did the Alderman mean? Did he mean that re- ceipts and profits were identical terms. If the Corpora- tion got half the receipts it meant chat the company was to make a hundred per cent, before they got a penny. Business might be good but not so good as that. (Laughter.) If the Corporation got half the profits, did that improve matters? Did it make the thing respectable? Not for a moment. What remedy had they against the advertising company if they did not treat thoee who hired the hall, properly ? They might go and grumble at them and have a row with them, but if they took the hall again, they most go and ask the company if they would undertake the advertis- ing again. It was not fair to the people who took the hall. It was croaked,and there were too many crooked things in connection with the Cerporation. If there was a crooked way it almost looked as if the Corporation were exceptionally quick in finding it out. It was a monopoly pum and simple. Proceeding to refer to Councillor F R Roberts, he said he was the gentleman who didn't preach the sermon about Lavern's, Limited. (Hear, hear.) Had they ever heard of the Irishman who got up and said. " Before I begin I wish to make a few remarks "1 (Laughter.) That was what Councillor F R Roberts did. He made these few remarks but didn't preach them. (Laughter.) He uttered them in the pulpit but they were not a part of the sermon. (Laughter.) Per- haps it was a good thing,for he preached on temperance and Councillor F R Roberts was most intemperate in his language when on this subject. Fle was speaking on January 7th at the Council meeting and admitted that the only mistake they made was in rimming that the remarks referring to Ingram's came after the text. That was what he (Mr Hulme) called a distinction without a difference. (Hear, hear.) After making that admission. Councillor Roberts said he wanted to " ecotch that snake and kill it." What about that other snake—the £2O snake ? (Laughter.) lie Mr Hulme) was afraid Councillor Roberts had scotched that snake and killed it dead. (Laughter.) For a charitable man Councillor Roberts was singularly slow in putting down his £2O for the Infirmary. (Laughter). Did they remember that lawyer' letter seat to Mr Norbury Williams ? Mr NORBURY WILLIAMS: I do. Mr HULMIS : It was about Ingram's, Limited. (Laughter.) In that letter Councillor Roberts said that lalr Norbury Williams' statement about Ingram's, Limi- ted. was an unmitigated lie. (Laughter). At the next meeting Mr Wiiliams proved that every word he had uttered respecting it was abselutely and perfectly true. Had they heard that Councillor Roberts had apologised or withdrawn that little staterneat ? Referring to the remarks in the Council Chamber, that members of thei Municipal Non-Trading Committee were not fit to sit on the committee of inquiry because they had prejudged the case, Mr Huhn° said he flatly contradicted it. A certain amount only of the evidence had been examined anl out of that certain cases of illegal trading had cropped up. Was it a case of pre-judging or a logical deduction to say that if the whole of the evidence were sifted more cases would be found. Alderman Roberts used a nasty little word. He described these meetings as being "packed." What did be mean. If he meant like herring in a barrel there was perhaps some truth in it. The Council seemed unable to discriminate between illegal and improper trading. If the Council had their way the first thing would be to turn it into a limited liability company. (Laughter.) They couldn't possibly help it. They need only extend the objectionable prac- tice relating to the letting of Parr Hall. Would not the Corporation make a lot more money if they made it apply to those who came into the hall? (Laughter ) Let them have a regulation whereby they would buy their boots) from so-and-so because they gave half the profits to the Corporation, and buy clothes from the Municipal Clothing Supply Association—Limited-e (laughter)—because they did the same. (Laughter.) He wined the Council to beware of the Ides of March. (Applause.) The Corporation might have little successes by the way and they might crow over them. Somebody crowed last nieht—(laughter)—but Ire had heard of men who had battled in adversity and afterwards in success. 'Applause). MR JOHN PEMBERTON AND THE SLANDER - ACTION.

REPETITION OF CHARGES AGAINST ALDERMEN. fd- Joan; Paranaarma, who was vociferously cheered on rising to speak, seconded the resolution. Be said that no doubt they had all heard of the action taken against him by Councillor " penny" Roberts. An im- portant point in the action which was not stated in the newspapers was that be was sued for £l,OOO damages— for wounded feelings—(laughter)—but a Lancashire apocial jury thought tbat the sum of £lOO was ample and sufficient. (A Voice : Too much). He wiahed to impress this upon them and he also wished them ti tell their friends that nrither that action nor its result bad had or would h ,Ye any effect on any part he was taking in the question of municipal trading. (Cheers.) At the meeting of the ' Town Council the previous night Councillor Bennett said he believed the agitation was •based to a largelex- teat upon a flimsy foundation. That was a very singu- lar assertion for Councillor Bennett to make because he was the only Councillor who had the alteration made in toe Standing Order referring to the opening of tenders What they (the Non-Tradieg Committee) proposed was that those contracts should be sealed and that they should be opened by the Chairman of the Committee in the presence of three members. Councillor Bennett had accepted the suggestions and very properly brought the motion before the Council and it had been accepted. And yet Councillor Bennett said he though-, their foundation was flimsy, but he had taken that nrcsssary precaution. Alderman Henry Roberts in his speech when he occupied the chair for the last time as Mayor of Warrineton,said he was glad to lay down his chain of 'office for the reason that he would be able to answer thnsa base insinuations made against him. Welawhere had he been ? (A voice : Manchester and laughter.) Where was ha, what had be answered what had he done and whet had he put right ? They knew that in his speech Alderman 12,berts made that famous £lOO challenge. He (the speaker) accepted it. Be stated it publicly there, he wrote to him by registered post, sent a copy of the letter to the newspapers and offered to take all the trouble to prove what he said in order that the Infirmary should get that £lOO, He had never heard a single word. (Laughter.) This gentleman was I going to clear all thes things away but there had not been a single word. He (the speaker) still hoped that Aldermaa Roberts would take up that challenge and give him the opportunity of earning that £lOO for the Infirm- ary.Efe:had:nothing to retract and he was perfectly willing to prove his charges whenever ho had the opportunity. But it must not be before a committee composed of four Town Councillors and two members of the Non-Trading Committee. He must refer again to that beautiful ser- mon especially to the teetotal part. (Laughter.) All the Roberts's were teetotalers and that was the reason there was so much hub-bob and so many people did not like them. (Laughter.) Mr Pemberton alluded to a company named Moses Walker and Sons Ltd., an ale and bottling company, and he found that Mr F Roberts was seta:lg as solicitor to that company. That was the way he supported this teetotal principles. Councillor Jolley had said definite charges had been made, and some of the members of that Corporation had been accused of illegal conduct and aceused of immoral conduct. But the law provided a way in which Such conduct could be dealt with, and provided penalties, whilst it also provided that the person who proved the offence should have half the penalty. No such action had been taken by the agitators to tenure those penal- ties. What was to prevent them. Be (Mr Pemberton) would tell them. The minutes of the Corporation and the orders for payment were kept in such a way that it was an absolute impossibility for any man on the facs'of this earth to gat the information in time. To lay infor- mation to take action by law they must lay the action within fourteen days from the cause, He said from that platform and with all sincerity that if the members of this Council whom ha charged with illegal trading wouldforego:that notice, be would take the summonses out to-morrow. (Cheers), If Alderman Shaw Green,
Alderman Francomb and Alderman Sutton would forego the notice required by law of fourtetn days he would bring actions against them_ to-morrow, _,(Loud cheers.)
MR. i'VELYLOR AND THE INQUIRY:

Mr R A NAYLOR WhO had a cordial reception, said he had travelled from Leaden in order to support the Chairman and those associated with him in the agita- tioa, which in his opinion was' a right one. (Applause.) The ratepayers had a perfect right to inquiry into the way the aff eirs of tha Borough are conducted. The inquiry seemed to him imperative and he was very much surprised at the members of the Warrington 'town Coencil setting their hacks against the inquiry he :ause it excited the suspicion of the ratepayers that there was something wrong somewhere. If there were no dark dealings why fear the light? (Hear, hear.) Truth and justice did not fear the search-light of investigation. (Hear, hear.) At this stage of the proceedings, Cluncillor WTLLOMa PIERPOINT entered the room and received an ovation. Mr NAYLOR (continuing) said he was pleased to see that they recognised the noble services of one member of the Warrington Town Council who wished to see fair play.(Applause.)What had the chairman to gain except the public good in making the sacrifice he had done and putting up with the ineults and the abuse that had been heaped upon him. (Hear, bar.) Then again what was Mr Pemberton going to gain over the transaction ? A VOICE: He is going to lose something. Mr NAYLOR: I don't think he will lose much. (Hear, hear.) Continuing he said be presumed the man in the , gallery thought Mr Pemberton would lose money. Money, what is money? He might lose a worse thing than money. (Hear, hear.) Whatever else Mr Pemberton lost, and he did not think he would lose morey—(hear, hear,)—he would not lose his manatees. (Applause). That was worth more than meney. (Laughter.) In referral; to the possible consequences of being struck off the list " of contractors to the Corporation, Mr Nay- lor paid be found that his margin of profit on Warring- ton Corporation contracte averaged 611 a week. (Laugh- 'for). He supposed that if he would only be quiet and it the gentlemen associated with him in business would onto cease from writing to the nowepepers or stirring up mud his firm would sill retain the honourable posi- tion of having the chance of sending in quotations to the Corporation which hitherto had been seld mm accepted. There was not a man or boy connected a ith him in trade whom he would ask to sell his manhood and his independence for 61i a week. (Applause.) He advised his hearers to remember at the next election all those men who had steadfastly declined to allow their conduct to be publicly investigated. Referring to the presence of a member of Parliament on the platform Mr Naylor said he hoped to be at the same job himself before long. (Applause). He advised members of the Town Council to be careful what they said about people outside. He was advised by a leading London barrister to take action against a certain member of the War- rington Town Council for defamation of character. A VOICE: Serve him right. Mr NAYLOR : The law of libel is very curious is it n'A Mr Pemberton ? (Laughter). Sometimes it was only a toss up who wins and who loses. At the same time it was not very nice for a man to get up in the Warrington Town Council and give a ratepayer such as he (Mr Naylor) was a little bit of graenitous blaek- guarding without any just cause to do it. Of course if he felt so inclined he could give that man a pretty severe castigation because the miserable attempt he made to exeilain away what was absolutely wrong and trying to make it right was open to very serious critic- ism. (Applause). Speeches were afterwards given by Mr Norbury Williams, and Mr R Cameron, Ml', who supported the resolution, which was unenimously carried.

div.head: Meeting in the Parr Hall.
div.p: Meeting in the Parr Hall.

Parr Hall was crowded with an enthusiastic audience on Wednesday evening on the occasion of another meeting under the auspices of the Municipal Non-Trading Committee. Mr James Dodds presided and he was supcorted on the plat- form by Messrs R Cameron, R A Naylor, S Norbury Williams, A Hulme, S Kenyon, John Pemberton and others. Mr Pemberton was warmls cheered when he took his seat on the platform as was also Councillor William Pierpoint. THE CHAIRMAN'S _SPESCH.

- The CHainasfetr, in the course of his remarks, said the resolution which was passed a month ago by the Council was a dishonest resolution. It stated what was not true. The Municipal Non-Trading Committee distinctly asked for a full inquiry into all the trading by members of the Council with the Corporation for the past five years.—Tne resolution read—" That as an inquiry has already been held." Was that true ? (" No.") It was not. The inquiry of what had been called "The White- washing Committee" of three Councillors was an in- quiry into what the elective auditor considered to be a few irregular payments made to three Aldermen—Green Sutton and Francomb, during the last financial year. The resolution went on to say that "any further inquiry is uaneceasary as it would lead to no beneficial result and would entail great expense on the town." A gentle- man, whese opinion he valued as much as that of any man in Warrington, said to him in relation to this that if a full inquiry cost £lo,ooo—(cheers)—it would be well-spent money and that the ratepayers would bo more than recouped within the next three years. (Ap- plause ), The resolution proceeded,—"On the other hand, if the ratepayers desire it and obtain the neces- sary sanction from the Local Government Board the Council would not oppose, Lec." Now listen to this. At last month's meeting the Town Clerk advised the Council that the Local Government Board would not indeed could nor, sanction, in fact had no power to sanction any inquiry. (Laughter.) Herein was the dishonesty of the resolution. In effect the Council said .—" We know the Non-Trading Committee cannot possibly get the Local &menu:pent Board to sanction any inquiry ; it will be quite safe to say so and so lead the public to think we are not afraid of an inquiry. Let us say," If you,the Non-Trading Committee can obtain the neceseary sanction of the Local Government Board we will not oppose." He said deliberately that that resolution was an insult to the ratepeyers —(cheers)—and was not creditable to those members of the Council who drafted it or who suppor;ecilit,from the top to the bottom Referring to the refusal of an inquiry, the CHAIRMAN said he expected nothing else, and from the Warrington Town Council, as it was at present constituted, they would get no fair or full inquiry. (Hear, hear.) The Municipal Non-Trading Committee had had two objects in this agitation ant' two only. First to prove that over the last five years there had been a very serious amount of illegal and immoral trading by members of the Coun- cil with the Corporation, and secondly, and mainly, to take such action as ehould secure that henceforth all such improper dealings, direct or through limited companies should be impossible. There was not a single cearge, there was not a single word that he had uttered in connection with this contreverey that he did not sten I by to the letter. The Council dare cot give an enquiry sash as they could accept, and such as they were entitled to, and the only solution open was that as they could not mend the exist- ing intolerable eituation they must end it, at the earliest moment, and in the only possible way ! They must go to the House of Comm, ne (Applause.) They must organize the ratepayers in every ward, they must fight the seat of every retiring member who had opposed their objects or who ha I been guilty of improper deal- ings with the Corporation during his expiring term, and in less than two years he hoped they might be in a position to stop all crooked dealings, and to prove to the hilt, by an impartial inquiry, the statements and the charges they had made. He had the Utmost sympathy with the Mayor. Like him, he was not anxious to show up the moral delinqueneie3 of others, indeed he had little liking for an inquiry. His sole object in desiring one was that it might be shown that all they had said was provable. The Mayor says he has seen nothing wrong so far. So also Alderman Monks. (Laughter). Oh ! yes, he says there have been very improper doings but they are now stopped. Were they ? (Laughter). If so, thanks to this committee. (Cheers). If not, and if this committee was to be dis- solved, how long would it be before matters were worse than ever before ? (Hear. hear). Mr Dodds proceeded to speak of the arrangement made by Alderman Roberts with regard to the profits of the Slate Company where' by, he said, he had no pecuniary interest in Corporation (Contracts. Mr ANDERTON : " Who has he given his interests tor The CHAIRMAN : That I cannot say, Continuing he said. Some of tiime Aldermen who had been named as having had irregular dealings with the Warrington Cor- poration were very indignant with the Non-Municipal Trading Committee and in particular Alderman Shaw Green asks, "Can any honourable man sit calmly whilst his good name and reputation are being recklessly assailed ?" He (the chairman) agreed indeed,he thought

div.head: NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.
By " Ovalist."

Footballers in the Warrington district were sadly disappointed on Saturday when the match with Salford was postponed owing to frost. Backword was sent to the Salfordians rather too early, for the sun shone with great power later in the day and by three o'clock in the afternoon the ground was in a by no means bad state. The weather could not have been better from a spectacular and playing point of view and it is a thou- sand pities that the match could not be brought off. The postponement, moreover, means a considerable loss to the club unless both teams are knocked out of the cup-ties early on and can arrange to play on some vacant Saturday.

One or two fixtures were successfully brought off. For instance at Broughton, Swinton accomplished a feat which every other Lancashire club had failed in attemp ing, by defeating the champions. The Rangers were clearly outwitted,and just now the Lions are going very strongly. At Hull, Bradford's long run of successes , was checked, for they only rranagea to draw with the Third Porters. Halifax continued on the up-grade and added the scalp of Leigh to their list of recent victims.

The monthly gatherings of the Northern League and ! Northern Union Committees wore held on Tuesday evening at Huddersfield. Warrington were consider- ably interested in the former, as no less than three of the first team players were up for various kinds of rough play. The two forwards got off lightly, Board- man escaping with a caution, and Swift with one week's suspension. Burgess, the unlucky, was more severely dealt with, and his suspension to the end of March is a severe blow to the Club. The charge a gainst him was that of kicking an opponent, and though Burgess was not altogether to blame, the fact of it being his second offence went against him. At any time the Flixton youth is hot-heasied and a bit too fond of " getting his own back." Still he has been hardly dealt with this season.
Burgess's suspension will probably keep him out of at least ten matches, and the loss to the club can hardly be estimated, especially as Allen is also hors de combat.

Swinton (for the second time) and Runcorn each had two points deducted for breach of the professional rules, while Hunslet look like being once more in the same uncomfortablelboat. They have infringed professional law 1 and will probably lose:two:more points next month Swinton's punishment robs them of the second Place, Bradford just beating them by a point.

The county match with Durham and Northumberland on Wednesday was a treat for the Lancashire players who gave the home team a lesson in scientific football such as will not be forgotten in South Shields for a long time. The full score was 49 points to 10 points in favour of the Palatine representatives. And yet the I match was a really excellent one. The home players made a better show than the score indicates, but it was the dazzling brilliancy of the Lancashire combina- ation which outclassed them. The passing movements were superb and hugely delighted the spectators who had never seen Rugby football of this kind before. W James played a wonderful game, and Fish was also in his best form, running in three beautiful tries behind the posts. He also kicked three goals, two from touch, while W James placed no less than eight goals —a re- markable performance.

Warrington pay another visit to Yorkshire to-day, their opponents being Huddersfield, who were defeated at Warrington by 5 Points to nil. They have done some smart things on their own ground this season, and he would be a bold man who predicted victory for War - rington, especially with both the regular halves away. After the victory at Hull, however, we need not be surprised at anything. .

--- The Warrinctton team will be as follows :—Hallam, full back ; Fish, Isherwood, Dickenson and Barris, threequarters • Duckworth and Edmonds half backs, Morrison, Boar'dman,.Fell, Edmondson, J Swift, Ashton, Taylor, and J Jolley, forwards. Allen is still unfit for play, and R Rate being so slow Duckworth has another chance to exhibit his prowess behind the pack.
